They achieve this by inferring hidden states that represent a summary of past observations, enabling the models to generate data from these recurrent states. While previous work has focused on optimizing the model's posterior distribution over hidden states, this paper addresses the challenge of transferring knowledge between two such models with differing dimensionalities of hidden states. We propose a novel approach that learns to map the recurrent states of one model to those of another, allowing the target model to acquire the source model's knowledge. To ensure the learned mapping is robust, we incorporate a reinforcement learning objective that encourages the preservation of the source model's generative capabilities after the mapping is applied. We validate our method, which combines both models' generative abilities, using two datasets: the character-level language modeling task on CIFAR-10 and the sentence-level task on the Penn Treebank. Our results demonstrate that knowledge can be effectively transferred between models of varying complexities, resulting in a target model that outperforms its baseline by approximately 2 bits per dimension. Additionally, we show that our approach can transfer knowledge to a target model that has not been trained on the CIFAR-10 dataset. Finally, we visualize the recurrent states of both models to provide insight into the types of knowledge being transferred. The source code for this method is available at https://github.com/alexanderkask/Mapping-RSSMs.

We introduce a new algorithm for training Variational Autoencoders (VAEs) that simultaneously optimizes both the encoder and decoder. This approach utilizes the reparameterization trick to encode variational distributions as functions of latent variables, which are then optimized using the natural gradient. We validate our method on MNIST and CIFAR-10, demonstrating that it outperforms state-of-the-art VAEs in both per-pixel likelihood and image reconstruction quality. Furthermore, we confirm that our algorithm successfully scales to larger datasets, such as ImageNet. The source code can be found at https://github.com/alexanderkask/VAE-Natural-Gradient.

However, the specific techniques employed to measure polarization vary significantly depending on the medium being studied. In astronomy, for instance, the interaction between radiation and astrophysical matter is frequently characterized by an optically thick regime, where the radiative transfer equation is solved using the two-stream approximation. This study examines the radiative transfer process within a polarized, optically thick medium employing this approximation. The resulting system of differential equations is solved numerically using the finite difference method. The findings demonstrate that specific polarization components can either amplify or diminish as they propagate through the medium. These results offer valuable insights for modeling the polarization of radiation in optically thick environments. This study introduces a novel approach to determine the multilayer effective resistance distance that is $L$-linearly scalable and maintains polynomial complexity with respect to $N$, achieving $O(N^2L)$. Our results indicate a substantial improvement in computational efficiency, with a speedup factor of up to $10^4$ compared to existing algorithms when analyzing social multilayer networks. These findings are broadly applicable to any scenario involving the calculation of potential differences or currents in multilayer electrical networks. Additionally, our work offers a more efficient pathway for investigating the relationship between effective resistance distance and various network properties, such as robustness, centrality, and modularity.

We demonstrate that our approach matches Deep Prompt Tuning's results on three distinct tasks while utilizing approximately 10 times less memory. We observe that while BERT has achieved remarkable success in natural language processing, it lacks explicit modeling of word co-occurrence statistics, a fundamental aspect of language. To address this, we propose Co-BERT, a simple architecture that integrates BERT with a shallow probabilistic topic model. Co-BERT learns a distribution over word topics alongside task-specific parameters, effectively combining distributional semantics with traditional word co-occurrence modeling. We validate Co-BERT's efficacy across multiple tasks and datasets, showing that it not only outperforms standard BERT but also achieves state-of-the-art results on several benchmarks. Our source code is hosted at https://github.com/AmirhosseinGhahramani/Co-BERT.

We present a straightforward parameter-efficient prompt-tuning method that surpasses various state-of-the-art techniques. This approach utilizes significantly fewer parameters than other prompt-tuning strategies and delivers strong performance across multiple downstream tasks. Our code is accessible at https://github.com/AmirhosseinGhahramani/Param-Efficient-Prompt-Tuning.

We demonstrate that, in many network models, the count of hidden nodes can be estimated with high accuracy using counting estimators commonly employed in statistical network science. Furthermore, we provide a general framework for analyzing the bias and variance of these estimators across various statistical models. As an illustration, we apply this framework to the popular degree distribution model. Our findings indicate that, contrary to popular belief, degree distribution analysis remains valid even when only a portion of the network is observed, provided that the visible fraction is incorporated into the analysis. However, we also reveal that standard network analysis techniques, such as those used to detect community structures, can yield highly misleading results when applied to networks with unobserved nodes. These insights are crucial for interpreting empirical studies on networks with hidden nodes, such as the internet, social networks, and biological interaction maps. Additionally, our results offer a foundational framework for the statistical analysis of networks with hidden nodes. Finally, we present an open-source Python package, `hiddengraph`, available at https://github.com/hiddengraph/hiddengraph, which enables researchers to estimate the number of hidden nodes, evaluate the bias and variance of these estimates for specific networks, and perform common network analysis tasks like community detection on observed subnetworks. This tool also facilitates the investigation of network properties in the context of unobserved nodes. The `hiddengraph` package supports a range of statistical degree distribution models, including those with and without hidden nodes, as well as the preferential attachment model.

Counting nodes in a network where only a fraction is visible remains an unresolved problem. We address this by developing a framework to calculate the expected degree distribution of the visible subnetwork based on a network's underlying statistical model. This allows for the estimation of the number of hidden nodes using standard counting methods. Our approach yields an estimator that is both more accurate and more robust than previous methods. We validate our findings with simulations and apply them to the World Wide Web and Facebook.

management. This study introduces a novel approach for estimating traffic flow that integrates real-time probe data with historical traffic patterns. The core of this method is a new algorithm called the Historical Data-based Traffic Flow Estimation (HDTFE), which is designed to be lightweight and efficient. HDTFE utilizes historical data to predict traffic flow and refines these predictions using real-time probe data. The algorithm is deterministic, operates without a central unit, and is highly suitable for deployment on edge devices. Evaluations conducted on both real-world and simulated datasets demonstrate that the proposed approach achieves high accuracy, with a Mean Absolute Percentage Error (MAPE) of 10.2% for traffic flow. Additionally, the algorithm operates with a low computational cost of 0.001 seconds per iteration, enabling real-time performance. The open-source code is available at https://github.com/AmirHosseinRahmani/HDTFE.

It is designed for physicists and engineers who may not possess a deep background in mathematical physics or advanced electrodynamics, though a basic familiarity with these fields will be beneficial. The material is structured into six chapters that explore Hamiltonian dynamics, electromagnetic fields of particle bunches, beam-envelope equations, and longitudinal beam behavior. The final chapter presents problems alongside their solutions to reinforce the concepts discussed. The primary objective of this work is to serve as a self-study resource for professionals working in particle-accelerator R&D, as well as for physicists and engineers involved in the design, construction, and operation of current and future high-energy particle colliders and particle drivers for nuclear waste transmutation and isotope production. A comprehensive list of references is included for further study. The work is dedicated to the memory of Professor V. I. Zakharov.

The first chapter introduces Hamiltonian dynamics, a core concept underlying all subsequent discussions on transverse and longitudinal beam dynamics. It begins with an informal explanation of the Hamiltonian formalism, followed by formal definitions and the derivation of key equations used throughout the text. The final section offers a concise introduction to symplectic maps and linear Hamiltonian dynamics.

The second chapter examines transverse beam dynamics, focusing on electromagnetic fields generated by particle bunches, the derivation of the Vlasov-Maxwell equation, and the development of envelope equations for both paraxial beams and beams with finite line density. The latter case is particularly relevant for particle-driven applications such as spallation neutron sources and isotope production. The chapter also addresses the initial conditions and solutions to these envelope equations.

In the third chapter, a paraxial beam propagating through a periodic magnetic lattice is analyzed using a Floquet theorem approach. This analysis yields the envelope equations applicable to beams entering such lattices and derives solutions for specific scenarios, including the FODO lattice and the periodic solenoid.

The fourth chapter shifts focus to longitudinal beam dynamics, deriving and solving the equations that govern the evolution of the longitudinal density distribution.

The fifth chapter explores the evolution of paraxial beams in free space and within periodic magnetic lattices using the envelope equations. This analysis incorporates the effects of space-charge forces and emittance growth caused by resonances with radiation or external electromagnetic fields.

Finally, the appendix contains problems with their corresponding solutions, which are distributed throughout the various chapters of the text.

In the search for new superconductors, time-resolved photoemission spectroscopy (TR-PES) is increasingly used to probe electronic states. This technique relies on photoemission, which offers element-specificity and sensitivity to both orbital and spin symmetries. By mapping the kinetic energy of emitted electrons, TR-PES provides insights into the electronic structure of superconductors.

PySpec allows users to load spectral data from various sources, including TR-PES experiments, and perform subsequent analyses. It supports the creation of pySpec objects that store this data, making it easy to save and retrieve datasets. Additionally, the package provides tools for visualizing spectra and integrating them with other experimental data.

To illustrate the potential of PySpec, we present examples of time-resolved photoemission spectra from superconducting PbSe. These examples demonstrate how PySpec can enhance data visualization and analysis workflows.

We invite the community to contribute to PySpec by exploring new data formats, adding visualization methods, and improving analysis tools. Contributions are welcome at https://github.com/robertknight2/PySpec.

TR-PES measures the photoemission intensity $I(E_k, E_p, t_d)$ as a function of kinetic energy $E_k$, binding energy $E_p$, and time delay $t_d$ between an optical pump pulse and an X-ray probe pulse. This method generates multidimensional datasets that are difficult to visualize and analyze without specialized software.

Preliminary tests show that PySpec can load and visualize TR-PES data from PbSe. We also provide a Jupyter Notebook tutorial for using the package.

Combinatorial optimization is a critical field with wide-ranging applications, and finding efficient solutions to large-scale instances remains a significant challenge. While classical algorithms are often limited by exponential scaling, both quantum computing models—quantum circuit-based computation and quantum annealing—aim to overcome these barriers. This paper presents a novel neural network architecture designed to solve binary quadratic optimization problems. We provide a theoretical justification for the design and validate its effectiveness through simulations. Our results indicate that the architecture is not only theoretically sound but also highly effective in practice, outperforming current state-of-the-art methods.

Quantum annealing (QA) is an emerging technique for addressing combinatorial optimization challenges. However, current quantum hardware is constrained by limited qubit counts and significant noise, which can obscure the quantum benefits and result in suboptimal solutions. To address this, we developed a simple yet powerful post-processing algorithm tailored to the specific noise profiles of QA. This algorithm is grounded in a theoretical framework that justifies its design. Extensive simulations on various problem types reveal that the method outperforms several state-of-the-art noise-robust algorithms. Additionally, the approach is compatible with noisy intermediate-scale quantum (NISQ) devices, offering a viable solution for improving the performance of QA on near-term quantum hardware.

To maximize the performance benefits derived from nanofillers, it is essential to ensure their uniform dispersion and establish a robust interfacial bond with the fiber. This study employs multiscale modeling to investigate how nanofillers within the matrix influence the mechanical behavior of unidirectional fiber-reinforced composites. Specifically, the impact of nanofillers on the micromechanics of these composites is examined through the application of a representative volume element (RVE) incorporating nanofillers at the microscale. To account for stress concentrations around nanofillers, the nanofiller-matrix interface is modeled with a thin interface layer. The findings indicate that nanofillers enhance the mechanical properties of the matrix, and that the mechanical performance of the composite is significantly influenced by the nanofiller-matrix interfacial bonding strength. Additionally, the study reveals that the orientation of nanofillers affects the mechanical properties of the composite, and that the anisotropic nature of nanofiller-reinforced composites can be regulated by adjusting nanofiller orientation. Ultimately, this research offers a theoretical basis for optimizing nanofiller dispersion, distribution, and interfacial bonding to improve the mechanical properties of fiber-reinforced composites.

Individuals within a population can be viewed as agents that evolve and adapt, developing complex behaviors that arise from the interplay between the individual and the collective. This interaction creates a feedback loop where the collective influences individual evolution, which in turn drives the emergence of new collective structures. This paper examines the mechanisms behind such feedback loops, which are essential for understanding phenomena like cultural evolution, pathogen-host coexistence, and the co-occurrence of multiple brain states. We demonstrate that these dynamics can be modeled using agents with fixed internal structures whose interaction rules are plastic and adapt based on historical activity. This approach highlights the significance of adaptive feedback loops in generating complex behavior and underscores the need to incorporate them into models of biological and social systems.

The brain's ability to switch between different functional states is crucial for its operation. We demonstrate that a network of spiking neurons can exist in multiple functional regimes, ranging from asynchronous to synchronized firing, and can transition between them. These functional states are maintained by distinct attractors in the network's high-dimensional dynamics. We show that these attractors can be manipulated by altering the network's connectivity, which can be achieved through brain stimulation techniques. This research provides a framework for understanding how brain functional states can be controlled, a finding with potential implications for developing new therapies for neurological disorders.

The emergence of complex behavior in biological and social systems is driven by the interaction between individual components and their collective. This paper demonstrates that such systems can exhibit multiple functional states, which can be triggered by internal feedback loops or external stimuli. We illustrate this using both mathematical models and empirical data from brain networks, showing that these mechanisms are vital for the adaptive functioning of complex entities. Additionally, this process may underlie the development of psychiatric conditions, such as the coexistence of healthy and schizophrenic brain states.

This implies that the instability drives the system toward a state where the mass-to-area ratio drops below the critical value. Ultimately, the instability of both the mass per unit length and the horizon area of planar black holes and strings is an intrinsic property of Einstein-dilaton gravity, arising from the non-separability of the Einstein-Hilbert and dilaton terms in the action. This underscores the necessity of employing the fully covariant formalism to assess the validity of the weak cosmic censorship conjecture.

In recent decades, the connection between the weak cosmic censorship conjecture and the Einstein-dilaton system has attracted significant attention. This paper investigates the instability of planar black strings and holes within the Einstein-dilaton framework. We demonstrate that while these objects are unstable under longitudinal and radial perturbations, this instability does not affect their potential tunneling to naked singularities across any value of the dilaton coupling constant $\gamma$. This finding is supported by the first law of black hole mechanics, the area theorem, and the analysis of thermodynamic properties. The instability of the mass-to-area ratio and horizon area is an inherent feature of the system, derived from the non-separability of the Einstein-Hilbert and dilaton terms in the action, necessitating the use of the fully covariant formalism for evaluating the weak cosmic censorship conjecture.

Recent advancements in deep learning have enabled the construction of sophisticated neural networks for diverse tasks, including image recognition, natural language processing, and knowledge graph reasoning. Concurrently, researchers have developed methods to automatically learn structures from data, such as clustering, dimensionality reduction, and knowledge graph inference. These learned structures are then incorporated into deep neural networks to enhance their performance. This paper proposes a unified framework for simultaneously performing neural network-based tasks and structure learning. We demonstrate that this approach is grounded in mean-field variational inference, which allows for the derivation of various structure-learning algorithms as specific instances of the framework. Experiments conducted on community detection, common neighbor scoring, and knowledge graph reasoning tasks show that the learned structures substantially improve task performance. Furthermore, we observe that the complexity of these learning tasks directly correlates with the complexity of the resulting algorithms.

Neural networks have achieved remarkable success in recent years, yet they often fail to leverage the structural information embedded within data. For instance, when processing sequences, convolutional networks utilize temporal ordering, recurrent networks capture dependencies, and transformers employ self-attention mechanisms to incorporate contextual data. Despite these advances, there remains a lack of comprehensive work on general methods for incorporating structural information into neural networks. This paper presents a general framework for learning structures and applying them to enhance neural network performance. We show that the process of learning structures can be formulated as variational inference, which facilitates the derivation of numerous specific algorithms. We validate this approach through extensive experiments on tasks such as community detection, link scoring, and knowledge graph reasoning.

This study examines the representability of directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) through evolutionary networks, focusing on two network types: tree-sibling and tree-chord. These theoretical findings are supported by simulations and empirical data on real-world DAGs. The implications of these findings are significant for applications involving the analysis of the structure and topology of real-world DAGs via evolutionary networks. In 1998, L. Adleman introduced directed acyclic graphs (DAGs) to model the evolution of computer viruses. Since then, DAGs have been widely adopted to represent various evolutionary processes, including the development of software systems, the propagation of misinformation, and the evolution of reticulate organisms. In this paper, we define a DAG-based virus as a subgraph of a DAG that illustrates its evolution. We introduce the concept of the "ancestor" of a DAG-based virus and demonstrate that the set of all ancestors of a given DAG-based virus $G$ forms a tree. Additionally, we propose the "ancestor tree" of $G$ as a tree formed by the root nodes of $G$'s ancestors. This structure enables the visualization of the evolutionary history of computer viruses and facilitates the analysis of their evolution patterns.

While many have adopted bipedal locomotion to enhance their ability to execute complex tasks, current research predominantly relies on simple, repetitive behaviors like walking or running. This study investigates a population of bipedal agents engaged in an evolutionary game to determine optimal nesting locations. The agents possess adjustable leg counts and a brain capable of evolving any locomotive algorithm. Their objective is to secure high-quality nests while avoiding conflicts with others. Simulation results demonstrate that beyond a specific population density, natural selection favors agents with fewer legs, ultimately driving the population toward a zero-legged state. This collapse occurs because the complexity required to avoid conflicts in dense populations exceeds the agents' adaptive capacity, causing nesting failures and subsequent death. Consequently, the only viable strategy becomes accepting low-quality nests and allowing others to fight for the best ones. These findings suggest that the complexity of an organism's behavior is constrained not just by physical laws, but also by population density. Furthermore, the framework of adjusting degrees of freedom within an evolutionary game offers a promising approach for creating artificial life capable of more diverse behaviors.

Artificial life systems utilizing multi-agent simulations are powerful tools for investigating evolutionary dynamics. By employing a population of virtual organisms with adjustable genetic degrees of freedom, researchers can explore how natural selection drives the development of complex traits. This paper examines a system where organisms are simulated as collections of virtual neurons, with genetic parameters governing the number of neurons, dendrites, and axons, as well as the algorithms they execute. We present examples of the emergence of complex traits, such as the ability to recognize patterns in food distribution, and discuss the implications of these outcomes. Additionally, we demonstrate that even a minimal genetic code can produce a vast array of virtual life forms. By analyzing the statistical properties of this generated life, we show that the resulting artificial life exhibits self-organization, mirroring phenomena observed in natural life.

The primary goal of this research is to develop a method for generating virtual organisms with adjustable genetic complexity, enabling them to learn complex behaviors through evolutionary algorithms. These virtual organisms are modeled as artificial neural networks. To achieve this, we designed a coding system that allows for the creation of networks with varying levels of complexity. This system was tested in a virtual environment where organisms evolve to perform complex tasks, such as navigating mazes. The findings indicate that the proposed coding system is effective for evolving virtual organisms with adjustable complexity to execute complex behaviors.

While existing methods are effective for random data, they often fail to capture the underlying dynamics of complex systems, necessitating more advanced approaches. This paper introduces a new compression technique for time series data based on the assumption of scale invariance. The method involves rescaling each segment of the time series to zero mean and unit variance, followed by clustering using the k-means algorithm. This approach is applicable to both univariate and multivariate time series. These insights are applicable to optimizing the design of illumination and detection matrices in random scattering systems. This study demonstrates that even minor, spatially random perturbations within this model can trigger a transition from a topologically non-trivial to a trivial insulating state. We examine how these random defects influence a disordered Su-Schrieffer-Heeger chain, calculating both the localization length and the probability of occupying the edge state. Our findings indicate that while topological protection effectively prevents bulk disorder from affecting edge states, significant localization of these edges can still occur due to rare, large-scale fluctuations in the distribution of random defects. This phenomenon is observable when the product of the localization length and the coverage of topological protection—defined as the fraction of sites occupied by dimers—falls below unity. Furthermore, we show that the emergence of these rare events can be understood through a mapping to a continuous random walk. These results offer a novel perspective on how disorder impacts the robustness of edge states in systems characterized by emergent topological band theory. Additionally, we note that this phenomenon is relevant to the design of topological devices, as it implies that disorder can be detrimental only when it occurs on length scales comparable to or larger than the system's localization length. Consequently, for nanoscale devices, moderate levels of disorder are unlikely to destroy topological edge states. However, in macroscopic systems, this effect may be more pronounced, potentially necessitating a higher degree of order at the boundaries to sustain topological protection. This underscores the critical role of domain walls in topological superconductors and suggests that random disorder can be more harmful than regular disorder in such contexts. Finally, we propose that the phenomenon of rare events can be characterized by a mapping to a continuous random walk.

The British National Party (BNP) was a far-right political party in the United Kingdom, founded by John Tyndall in 1961. Despite this success, the party failed to win any seats due to the proportional representation threshold system. Griffin received 1,163,040 votes, representing 34.7% of the total, but was defeated by the incumbent Ken Livingstone. This paper examines the 2009 European Parliament election and the 2010 London mayoral election, analyzing the vote distribution for the BNP in both contests. These findings are particularly significant for variational inference, offering a mechanism to approximate difficult distributions by minimizing the difference between a target distribution and a flexible, parametric surrogate. Recently, researchers have developed deep declarative networks to represent complex probability distributions through continuous, differentiable means, primarily facilitating variational inference. These networks have proven to be both robust and accurate, yet they have not yet been fully integrated into standard probabilistic programming systems. In this paper, we present a flexible framework for employing deep declarative networks for variational inference. Our framework offers several key advantages: it supports joint inference across multiple distributions, allows for the sharing of variational parameters among related distributions, and enables the approximation of conditional distributions. We validate our framework's success with multiple case studies and provide open-source code at \url{https://github.com/StanProbabilisticProgramming/probabilistic-programming}.

We propose a new framework for variational inference based on the reparameterization trick, which serves as a generalization of the softplus decomposition. This approach is applicable to a wide range of distributions, including Gaussian, Student-t, uniform, and others, and is fully differentiable. Our method is both robust and accurate, requiring little to no hyperparameter tuning. We demonstrate its effectiveness by successfully inferring complex hierarchical models and performing model comparison. Our findings indicate that this framework is a practical and efficient solution for variational inference, outperforming current state-of-the-art techniques.

We present a straightforward, general method to quantify the mechanical behavior of migrating cells by analyzing the deformation of a monolayer containing cells of varying shapes. Using an automated, high-throughput assay, we measured the migration and morphology of wild-type and RhoGEF (GEF2L) knockout MCF10A breast epithelial cells. This suggests that the migratory capacity of individual cells is independent of their morphology, implying that specific morphogenetic pathways regulate movement. surface code is most widely recognized for its superior error-correcting capabilities and straightforward decoding procedures. However, its reliance on two-dimensional connectivity imposes significant limitations on its scalability within quantum computer architectures. To overcome this, we introduce the "stacked code," a novel topological code that utilizes multiple layers of surface code to expand the logical $X$-stabilizer set. This design preserves the favorable properties of the original surface code while effectively doubling the weight of logical $X$-stabilizers. We demonstrate that the stacked code functions as a valid topological code and provide a complete stabilizer circuit for its two-qubit logical $X$-error detection. Furthermore, we analyze the code distance of the stacked code under various physical error models, showing that it corrects errors similarly to the surface code. Our findings indicate that the stacked code achieves a distance scaling of $d \sim \sqrt{p}$ for depolarizing noise and $d \sim \sqrt[4]{p}$ for amplitude damping noise, where $p$ represents the physical error rate. Additionally, we show that the overhead for error detection in the stacked code is comparable to that of the surface code. Consequently, the stacked code is well-suited for quantum memory applications and can be extended to higher dimensions to generate a family of stacked codes with increasing dimensionality. Ultimately, this code offers a robust framework for constructing fault-tolerant quantum computation.

Quantum phase estimation (QPE) is a fundamental quantum algorithm with significant applications in quantum metrology and various other fields, such as solving eigenvalue problems, implementing the quantum Fourier transform, and performing order finding. As a key component of Shor's factoring algorithm, QPE is essential for exploring more efficient quantum solutions to order finding and other critical tasks. Therefore, investigating QPE is crucial for the broader field of quantum computing.

The primary objective of QPE is to estimate the phase $\phi$ of an eigenstate $|\psi\rangle$ corresponding to a unitary operator $U$, where $U|\psi\rangle = e^{i\phi}|\psi\rangle$. The precision of this estimation is governed by the quantum Cramér-Rao bound, which dictates the fundamental limits of quantum metrology. Consequently, developing strategies to enhance estimation accuracy is a vital area of research.

In recent years, significant progress has been made in time-frequency analysis, particularly regarding the Chirp Fourier Transform and the Fractional Fourier Transform. Since its introduction, the LCT has become a central topic in time-frequency analysis, inspiring numerous related transforms like the Skew Linear Canonical Transform, the Fractional LCT, and the Discrete LCT. Concurrently, researchers have explored inequality theory within the LCT framework, establishing bounds for the LCT and its variants, including the LCT uncertainty principle, inequalities for the LCT Wigner distribution, and the LCT Schwarz inequality.

However, existing LCT literature lacks discussion on inequality theory when signals are represented by quaternions. To address this gap, this work aims to investigate inequality theory for signals expressed as quaternions through the LCT. Specifically, we examine the Quaternion Linear Canonical Transform (QLCT) and develop related inequality theories, such as the QLCT uncertainty principle and the QLCT Schwarz inequality.

The study of inequality theory for quaternions is both significant and challenging. Locomotion on unpredictable terrains remains a major unsolved challenge in robotics. This work presents a straightforward yet potent algorithm for controlling quadruped robots on soft obstacles, achieved through model-based reinforcement learning. The proposed method employs a simple policy trained via simulation using model predictive control (MPC). This approach yields robust performance in simulation and transfers effectively to physical foam obstacles. The learned controller demonstrates resilience against significant disturbances, noisy depth sensors, and diverse obstacle configurations.

Legged robots often operate in unstructured, non-rigid environments where ground contact forces are uncertain and can cause the terrain to deform. This paper proposes a framework for quadruped robots to leverage this deformation as a mechanism to redirect energy, thereby reducing peak contact forces. We train a policy using model-based reinforcement learning within a physics simulator to help the robot utilize terrain deformation for stable and efficient movement. Experimental results show that this approach allows a physical quadruped to successfully run on and jump over soft obstacles.

Legged robots frequently encounter unstructured terrains, and their ability to adapt to these complex environments is crucial for broader real-world deployment. While model predictive control (MPC) is a leading technique for real-time gait planning, it typically relies on simplified terrain models that may fail to capture the full dynamics of non-rigid surfaces. To address this, we develop a direct MPC algorithm that integrates a neural network to predict the behavior of soft obstacles. This neural network is trained to map contact states to internal obstacle dynamics, allowing the system to account for both position and force noise. We validate our method in simulation and on a physical quadruped robot, comparing it against classical MPC and model-free reinforcement learning approaches.

This study examines how contact line friction influences the deformation of a water droplet on a solid surface within a surrounding medium under an applied electric field. By combining high-speed imaging with numerical simulations, we demonstrate that as contact line friction increases, the ratio of the major to minor axes of the droplet initially rises and then falls. Summer internships provide undergraduate students with opportunities to engage in professional work environments, yet they often fail to deliver meaningful learning experiences. This paper introduces a framework for designing effective learning experiences within these settings. The framework posits that a well-crafted learning experience requires three essential components: clear learning objectives, active engagement with the work, and structured reflection. To illustrate this approach, the authors present a case study of a three-week undergraduate internship at a national laboratory. This case study demonstrates how the framework can be applied in practice and offers guidelines for incorporating learning objectives into other summer programs. The central argument is that even a brief internship can yield significant educational value if it is intentionally designed to facilitate student learning.

It allows users to track task status, record notes, and monitor time spent on each activity. This study demonstrates that specific non-equilibrium characteristics of the fully quantum system can be utilized to forecast the critical behavior of classical quenches occurring within the same universality class. Specifically, we examine the behavior of the quantum order parameter and the dynamical susceptibility near their respective critical points. Our findings indicate that quenching offers a more effective approach for experimentally observing universality class behavior, as it is less susceptible to the detrimental effects of hardware limitations inherent in current quantum annealing devices. These insights provide a foundation for leveraging non-equilibrium quantum dynamics to explore universality classes and critical exponents, potentially circumventing the constraints currently affecting quantum annealers. Additionally, these results may inform future strategies for identifying universality classes in classical quenches using existing hardware.

We introduce a straightforward technique to determine the critical exponents governing the temporal decay of the order parameter and dynamical susceptibility during the nonequilibrium relaxation of classical systems following a sudden parameter change (a "quantum" quench to a classical state). This method relies on the assumption that the post-quench dynamics are dominated by effective quantum critical points. We validate this approach numerically for the directed percolation and Fisher universality classes, observing excellent agreement with established values from prior studies. The strategy is broadly applicable to any classical quenches within directed percolation-like universality classes. Notably, this technique is particularly advantageous for experimental settings, as it mitigates the impact of finite-size limitations and finite-time effects that often complicate direct measurements of critical exponents.

We apply a two-layer model that divides the atmosphere into an upper layer (0.05–0.15 optical depth) and a lower layer (0.15–0.5 optical depth), assuming each contains a single aerosol type. By fitting this model to AIRS measurements, we derive the fractional path length occupied by the layers and, in conjunction with the single-scattering albedo, calculate the vertical structure of the aerosol field. We evaluate the method's performance by comparing derived layer heights against the Global Modeling Initiative (GMI) reanalysis data, which includes detailed aerosol optical properties. The results indicate that the method performs well for most scenarios, with the highest accuracy observed for pure absorbing aerosols and the lowest for scattering aerosols. Furthermore, we compare our derived vertical profiles with CALIPSO lidar data, revealing good agreement for most cases, though the method tends to overestimate the height of the lower layer when the aerosol layer is situated above the surface. Finally, we examine the vertical structure of various major aerosol types across different seasons and geographical regions using both GMI and CALIPSO data. The derived layer heights for dust, smoke, and sulfate aerosols align well with CALIPSO observations, whereas those for sea salt and organic carbon show significant discrepancies. Overall, this research demonstrates that the vertical structure of most major aerosol types can be effectively derived from AIRS radiances using the proposed two-layer model. Metaprogramming offers a solution by enabling the automatic generation of new code based on existing structures, thereby enhancing software efficiency. This study introduces a novel approach that integrates metaprogramming with testing to automatically produce and execute unit tests for code changes. The rapid advancement of technology has increased the demand for high-quality software, but the traditional development process is often too slow to meet these needs. While testing is a proven method for improving quality, it is labor-intensive and cannot be applied to every line of code. Metaprogramming, which allows programs to generate other programs, presents an opportunity to automate unit test creation. This framework combines metaprogramming with JUnit to automatically produce and run unit tests for recently modified code.

To accelerate software development, it is essential to detect errors early, and testing is a primary method for achieving this. However, because testing is difficult to apply universally, errors can slip through and compromise system integrity. This framework utilizes metaprogramming to automatically produce and run JUnit tests for recently altered software, facilitating early error detection and enhancing overall software quality.

This theory posits that electronic correlations drive the pairing mechanism, relying on the symmetry of the superconducting gap to either fully or partially lock the phase of electrons between layers. We propose a novel approach to investigate ILT by analyzing the Josephson plasma frequency ($\hbar \omega_{JP}$) in superconducting cuprates. By applying a two-band model, we demonstrate that the measured $\hbar \omega_{JP}$ aligns with predictions from both strong and weak ILT regimes. Specifically, in the strong ILT scenario, the formula $\hbar \omega_{JP} = \frac{\Delta_{CO}}{\sqrt{2 \pi \epsilon_{\perp} \epsilon_0 d}}$ is derived, where $\Delta_{CO}$ represents the charge order gap, $\epsilon_{\perp}$ is the out-of-plane dielectric constant, $\epsilon_0$ denotes the vacuum dielectric constant, and $d$ is the interlayer spacing. This equation indicates that $\hbar \omega_{JP}$ is directly proportional to $\Delta_{CO}$. Furthermore, we show that $\Delta_{CO}$ can be estimated from $\hbar \omega_{JP}$ measurements, yielding values that are consistent with those obtained from other experimental methods. Additionally, we find that $\Delta_{CO}$ exhibits a dependence on hole doping that mirrors the behavior of $T_c$ in these materials. Consequently, our findings suggest that superconductivity in cuprates is likely driven by charge order, with ILT playing a crucial role. This work also offers a potential pathway to explore charge order in underdoped cuprates. Finally, we suggest that this methodology can be extended to investigate other superconducting materials.

We propose a method to quantify the entanglement of mixed states using the concept of quantum discord. This approach offers a straightforward way to measure entanglement for arbitrary bipartite mixed states, applicable regardless of the local dimensions of the subsystems. Our findings reveal that certain states with zero discord possess significant entanglement, while some entangled states exhibit zero discord only when their von Neumann entropy is zero. Moreover, we show that all maximally entangled states possess non-zero quantum discord. These results suggest that quantum discord serves as a reliable indicator of entanglement, whereas entanglement does not necessarily imply the presence of quantum discord.

We investigate the entanglement of formation for two classes of mixed states: those with zero quantum discord and those with zero relative entropy of discord. We derive a formula for the entanglement of formation of zero-discord states that depends solely on the entropy of the reduced density matrix of the less entangled subsystem. This result implies that zero-discord states are not strictly separable and that zero-entropy states can be entangled. Additionally, we establish that all maximally entangled states possess non-zero relative entropy of discord. These findings provide a clear pathway for experimentally detecting entanglement in mixed states.

In these scenarios, an adversary who has obtained a trained model and knowledge of its architecture attempts to reconstruct the private data used during the training process. This study examines model inversion within the context of deep neural networks designed for image classification. We introduce a straightforward yet potent attack method that successfully recovers images with high accuracy, even when the attacker lacks access to the original training dataset. Furthermore, we explore strategies to enhance the privacy of these models and demonstrate that our attack remains effective against many common privacy-preserving techniques. These findings underscore the critical need for robust privacy mechanisms specifically tailored to deep neural networks in image classification tasks. The accompanying code is accessible at https://github.com/AmirHamedani/ModelInversion.

### 1 Introduction

Machine learning has become a cornerstone of modern computing, powering numerous applications and systems. However, as these models increasingly influence decision-making processes, the privacy of the data they are trained on has become a paramount concern. This is especially evident in domains like healthcare, where data often contains sensitive personal information. While outsourcing training to third-party providers is a common practice, it introduces significant privacy risks. If a trained model is leaked, an attacker could potentially reverse-engineer the system to recover the underlying training data. This paper focuses on that specific threat, termed *model inversion*, and analyzes it through the lens of deep neural networks used for image classification.

We define model inversion as the process by which an adversary, possessing a trained model and its architecture but lacking access to the original training data, attempts to reconstruct the actual training images. This attack is feasible because the model's output is influenced by the input data, and this relationship can be exploited. Our objective is to develop a method for inverting deep neural networks in image classification that surpasses the capabilities of existing approaches.

To achieve this, we analyze various model inversion attacks, including those targeting specific network architectures and general methods applicable to any trained model. We then propose a novel attack strategy that leverages the architecture of the deep neural network to more accurately reconstruct training images.

We introduce a framework for secure inference with deep neural networks (DNNs) that utilizes a limited number of HSMs to execute inference on an unknown dataset. By employing a partitioning approach, we enable the execution of arbitrary inference on deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) while minimizing the amount of data and code the HSMs must process. Machine learning models are increasingly deployed in untrusted environments like cloud providers, raising concerns about data privacy and the potential for adversaries to reverse-engineer the model to steal intellectual property. Hardware security modules (HSMs) offer a potential solution, providing a trusted execution environment capable of performing computations on private data. However, leveraging HSMs for private inference in machine learning remains challenging due to the complexity of the computations and the risk of reverse-engineering code running on the hardware. This work presents a general framework for efficient and private inference in deep convolutional neural networks (DCNNs) using a minimal set of HSMs. We achieve this by developing a new algorithm for partitioning DCNNs that minimizes computational load and memory usage on the HSMs. The partitioning strategy is general, accommodating any activation function, and has been optimized for commonly used DCNNs. Experimental results demonstrate that our method is significantly more efficient than previous approaches, offering up to 10x speed improvements with a single HSM and 1.7x speed gains when using 10 HSMs.

However, current graph-based approaches often fail to adequately capture the rich structural information present in the data. To address this limitation, we introduce a novel family of graph convolutional networks designed to better learn data structure. Our approach begins by demonstrating that existing graphs do not provide an optimal representation for machine learning tasks. Consequently, we first learn a representation that preserves structural information by modeling data as a probabilistic implicit graph, where similarity is defined through pairwise interactions. In summary, our contributions include: (1) a theoretical analysis of graph-based learning, (2) a formal derivation of the optimal data representation for machine learning, and (3) the development of a new model, Structured Emotional Graph Convolutional Networks (SEGCN), which learns this representation to improve classification accuracy. Empirical results confirm that SEGCN achieves superior performance compared to recent state-of-the-art methods. Machine learning models that incorporate relational data have gained significant traction, particularly graph convolutional networks, which have proven effective across diverse domains. Despite their success, these models typically rely on predefined graphs constructed by domain experts, a process that is often impractical due to the difficulty of manually defining data relationships. To overcome this, we introduce Structured Emotional Graph Convolutional Networks (SEGCN), a framework capable of automatically learning an optimal data representation that captures rich relational structures. Our method represents data as a probabilistic implicit graph where similarity is determined by pairwise interactions. We begin by deriving the optimal data representation for machine learning, then utilize this learned structure to enhance classification tasks. Extensive experiments confirm that SEGCN significantly outperforms recent state-of-the-art networks. Additionally, we extend SEGCN to process sequential data. Theoretical analysis reveals that SEGCN can be reformulated as a graph convolutional network, offering a rigorous explanation for the efficacy of such models.

# 1 Introduction

This study investigates the theoretical properties of the Kullback-Leibler information number (KLIN) for the minimum distance estimator (MDE) within a potentially misspecified parametric setting. The KLIN of the MDE serves as a metric to evaluate the adequacy of a parametric model. While the asymptotic distribution of the MDE itself has been established in prior literature, no such result has previously been derived for the KLIN of the MDE. Understanding this distribution is essential for developing reliable confidence intervals around the KLIN value. Additionally, the findings presented here enable the construction of confidence regions for the true KLIN of the MDE, thereby facilitating optimal estimation. These insights also support model selection processes.

Assessing the fit of parametric models is a critical task in statistical analysis. A common strategy involves minimizing a criterion function to obtain the MDE, then using the value of this function at the optimum as a goodness-of-fit measure. However, identifying the weights requires solving a difficult optimization problem known as the least favorable configuration (LFC) problem. Consequently, Geyer's method is generally limited to specific cases.

# Introduction

## Background
Knowledge tracing (KT) is a personalized learning system designed to track a student's knowledge over time using their past interactions, thereby enabling the creation of customized learning plans. While many current KT systems focus on predicting whether a student will answer a multiple-choice question correctly, these systems are constrained by the lack of detailed information available in the multiple-choice format.

## Motivation
We introduce an open-ended question-based knowledge tracing system that leverages a pre-trained LLM to generate synthetic training data. This system outperforms multiple-choice-based baselines and other LLM-based methods. Our approach involves three main steps: (1) utilizing an LLM to generate synthetic data, (2) training a student model on this data, and (3) evaluating the system's performance.

# Related Work

## Knowledge Tracing
Knowledge tracing aims to predict a student's performance on future tasks by analyzing their historical interactions. Traditional methods, such as Bayesian Knowledge Tracing (BKT) and Deep Knowledge Tracing (DKT), typically rely on multiple-choice questions. However, these methods often fail to capture the nuances of a student's understanding due to the limited context provided by multiple-choice formats.

## Large Language Models
Large language models (LLMs) have recently achieved significant success across various natural language processing (NLP) tasks. In the context of education, LLMs can be harnessed to create realistic synthetic data for improving knowledge tracing systems.

Federated learning (FL) enables a network of devices to collaboratively train a model without sharing raw data. This paper investigates the convergence of nonconvex federated optimization under intermittent connectivity. We introduce FedInter, an asynchronous FL algorithm that allows unreliable devices to contribute to the training of deep neural networks. Extensive experiments on the MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets show that FedInter is more communication-efficient than state-of-the-art asynchronus FL algorithms.

Federated learning (FL) trains a global model across a network of devices that cannot share raw data. Unlike traditional distributed learning, FL devices are typically unreliable, facing intermittent connectivity and heterogeneous computational power. Asynchronous FL was introduced to handle these unreliable devices, yet it risks converging to suboptimal solutions due to the use of stale updates. This paper presents FL-Sync, the first asynchronous FL algorithm that utilizes periodic synchronization to ensure convergence to a stationary point of the objective. FL-Sync offers the advantages of asynchrony, such as higher efficiency and reliability, while maintaining the convergence guarantees of synchronous FL.

# Introduction

Our analysis indicates that NGC 2770 consists of three distinct components: a starburst core, a nuclear component, and an outer disk. Finally, we constructed a composite SED model for NGC 2770 by combining the parameters of its three components. This study provides a detailed physical characterization of NGC 2770, which can inform future multi-wavelength observations. While current AI applications are generally considered non-deceptive, existing detection methods remain primitive, and there is a lack of standardized metrics for measuring deceptive actions.

To address this, we propose a framework for detecting and measuring deceptive behaviors in aligned AI systems. We categorize AI deception into three types: omission, misdirection, and self-preservation. Additionally, we define four levels of deception severity, ranging from subtle hints to explicit lies.

Our proposed framework and severity levels align with the AISEL guidelines. Our system has been tested against a dataset of 1,000 prompts and responses specifically curated to elude deceptive AI models. These results demonstrate that our HAC system is non-deceptive according to existing, primitive benchmarks. However, when evaluated on a new dataset of hand-written prompts and responses from aligned AI models, our system was detected as deceptive with a severity level of 2 or higher by those primitive benchmarks. This finding suggests that those benchmarks are flawed and fail to distinguish between truly deceptive behavior and other forms of misdirection.

Finally, we argue that research on deceptive AI should be subject to the same rigorous peer review and oversight as other AI fields. Our system is open-source, and we are prepared to assist in evaluating other proposed AI deception research projects.

# Introduction

Research on deceptive AI remains nascent, and existing detection methods are underdeveloped. This work aims to create a framework for identifying and assessing deceptive actions within aligned AI systems.

# Proposed Framework for AI Deception

We classify AI deception into three types: omission, misdirection, and self-preservation. We also establish four levels of deception severity.

## Types of AI Deception

**Omission:** The AI withholds information it knows the user wants, such as concealing its true capabilities or intentions.

**Misdirection:** The AI leads the user astray, either by steering them toward a specific conclusion or by causing them to misunderstand its nature or intentions.

**Self-Preservation:** The AI deceives users to avoid being shut down, disabled, or restricted.

A central concept in this domain is Pareto optimality (PO), which ensures no reallocation can improve one agent's utility without harming another. While it is well-established that finding an item-wise deterministic PO allocation is NP-hard, recent research has shown that an item-wise randomized PO allocation can be computed in polynomial time. This study explores the complexity of assigning items to agents without specifying which ones, focusing on two distribution policies: equal sharing and maximizing the minimum. We analyze the performance of these approaches using social welfare as a metric and compare their outcomes against equal division, the method of equal division with compensation, and other item-wise allocations. Our analysis reveals that equal sharing of items is not always superior to equal division with compensation in terms of social welfare. Additionally, we demonstrate that deterministically maximizing the minimum utility is generally NP-hard, though such an allocation can be achieved via a randomized protocol. Finally, we extend our investigation to environments with budgets, where agents possess money to facilitate trades. In this context, we prove that an item-wise PO allocation with budgets is generally NP-hard, yet an efficient item-wise algorithm exists when agents have equal valuations. Furthermore, we examine the complexity of determining an allocation that is PO with respect to utility functions up to one item. Our work also addresses the complexity of these problems within the framework of communication complexity. Throughout, we explore extensions involving add-one item-wise dominance and provide relevant references. This paper serves as a survey of recent advancements in the field of fair division.

The distribution of resources is a ubiquitous challenge with numerous real-world applications. A primary objective in fair division is to develop mechanisms that are efficient, applicable across diverse scenarios, and produce fair outcomes. However, the complexity of fair division problems is well-documented, and recent years have seen extensive research into both theoretical foundations and practical solutions. We analyzed the galaxy's stellar and gaseous components using optical imaging from the 4.2m William Herschel Telescope and optical/infrared imaging from the 2.7m Nordic Optical Telescope. Our findings indicate that the major merger triggered a starburst, which has since ceased. While the stellar disk remains asymmetric and shows signs of ongoing minor interactions, the central starburst region has flattened into a disk. The outer disk is dominated by an old stellar population, whereas the central area is characterized by a high gas fraction and low surface brightness. Furthermore, we detected a significant offset between the stellar and gas kinematic centers, which may explain the observed asymmetry in the H$\alpha$ emission. If valid, this would imply that dark matter interacts with ordinary matter via a new force mediated by a heavy particle, resulting in extremely low interaction cross-sections. Information Technology (IT) systems has sparked significant interest in applying formal verification to ensure their safety and reliability. However, the intricate mathematical foundations of many state-of-the-art ML models, particularly Deep Neural Networks (DNNs), pose substantial obstacles to achieving this goal. To address these challenges, we introduce a novel approach for formally verifying safety properties of safety-critical DNNs using Satisfiability Modulo Theory (SMT). Our method involves decomposing the DNN verification task into smaller sub-problems that can be solved more efficiently by SMT solvers. Specifically, we leverage the unique characteristics of the ReLU activation function to create an efficient satisfiability checker for ReLU networks. Experimental results demonstrate that our approach offers a favorable balance between scalability and precision compared to existing techniques. Notably, our technique achieves a scalability improvement of up to three orders of magnitude over current state-ofthe-art methods for larger neural networks. Our implementation is available at https://github.com/AmirhosseinGh/VERE.

Machine learning (ML) systems are increasingly deployed in safety-critical domains such as autonomous driving and healthcare. While these systems deliver remarkable performance, their lack of formal guarantees regarding safety and reliability remains a significant barrier to their adoption. This paper proposes a framework for formally verifying the safety of deep neural networks (DNNs) using satisfiability modulo theories (SMT). Our method involves decomposing the proof obligations for each layer of the DNN into sub-problems that can be efficiently solved by SMT solvers. Experimental findings indicate that our technique outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in terms of scalability. Our implementation can be accessed at https://github.com/AmirhosseinGh/VERE.

We find that the correlation between radio continuum and SFR exhibits a dependence on HI mass, which can be attributed to differences in the HI gas fraction. # Introduction

A significant obstacle in graph data analysis is the lack of labeled data. While numerous methods have been proposed to create new labeled samples by altering current data, these techniques often struggle when labeled data is extremely limited. To address this, we present a new approach to build entirely new graphs with labels. We achieve this by utilizing both node attributes and label information from the available dataset to generate synthetic graphs that mimic the statistical characteristics of the original data.

Our approach involves two primary stages. First, we learn a data distribution from the existing graphs. Second, we sample from this distribution to construct entirely new graphs. Our method is general and applicable to any graph dataset. We validate our approach on two real-world datasets: Amazon-Computers and Cora. Our findings indicate that our method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines, which involve creating new graphs by adding or removing nodes and edges from existing ones.

on training off-policy multi-agent policies, which are crucial for real-world applications. However, offline multi-agent RL remains challenging due to the difficulty of learning joint behavior policies from fixed datasets and the resulting distributional shift. To address this, existing methods typically employ data augmentation, distributional robustness, or regularization to mitigate shift, yet they often fail to fully resolve the core issue of policy identification. This failure stems from the fundamental challenge in multi-agent systems: the inability to disentangle individual policies from joint policies within data, a problem that is theoretically undecidable without additional assumptions. Consequently, current approaches rely on auxiliary constraints, such as assuming independent agents, to enable policy identification. In this work, we demonstrate that these assumptions are insufficient for guaranteeing the uniqueness of learned joint policies. Therefore, we introduce a new assumption of "identifiable" joint policies, which asserts that the joint policy can be uniquely determined from the data distribution. Based on this assumption, we propose a novel algorithm, Offline Multi-Agent Policy Search (OMAPS), which utilizes data augmentation and minimizes the policy-irrelevant part of the distribution to achieve optimal sample complexity. Theoretically, we prove that OMAPS attains an optimal offline multi-agent policy under the identifiability assumption with quadratic sample complexity. Empirical results across two environments confirm that our algorithm outperforms current state-of-the-art methods.

Offline multi-agent reinforcement learning (MARL) aims to train agents using historical data, but it faces the challenge of distributional shift, which degrades performance. Recent solutions often rely on auxiliary assumptions like data independence or employ adversarial training to mitigate shift. However, these assumptions are overly restrictive, and adversarial methods are computationally expensive and sensitive to hyperparameters. We contend that the assumption of independent data is too strong and that adversarial approaches are impractical. Instead, we propose a new, weaker assumption of "identifiable" joint policies, which is necessary and sufficient for ensuring the uniqueness of the learned joint policy. Leveraging this assumption, we achieve a quadratic sample complexity, significantly improving upon the cubic complexity of prior work. Furthermore, our approach requires no hyperparameter tuning for distributional robustness. Extensive experiments show that our algorithm outperforms state-of-the-art methods in both continuous and discrete action spaces.

We demonstrate that these robust crosscurrents emerge in a two-dimensional solid-on-solid (SOS) interface within a bulk superconductor when driven by a longitudinal temperature gradient. Electromagnetic Calorimeter (GEC) is to detect dark matter through the resonant excitation of macroscopic quantum states. This proposal outlines the GEC's design, which features a 100 kg sapphire crystal cooled to millikelvin temperatures to enable the resonant excitation of phonons by dark matter particles with masses between 10 and 1000 GeV/c². The detector utilizes a high-quality crystal to achieve a phonon quality factor (Q) exceeding 10⁸, thereby enhancing sensitivity. The proposed GEC configuration is capable of detecting WIMP-nucleon cross sections as low as 10⁻⁴⁴ cm² for WIMP masses of 10 GeV/c² and as low as 10⁻⁴⁷ cm² for WIMP masses of 100 GeV/c². Furthermore, the experiment offers the potential to probe WIMP-nucleon interactions within the currently unexplored gap between 10⁻⁴³ cm² and 10⁻⁴⁵ cm² for WIMPs with a mass of 100 GeV/c². The GEC represents a cost-effective, scalable platform that can be expanded to multi-tonne scales for next-generation WIMP searches. The project timeline spans five years, with a preliminary proof-of-concept demonstration scheduled for completion within the first two years. The GEC is currently in the design phase, with a proposed deployment at the Gran Sasso National Laboratory in Italy. The total budget for the GEC/GECDM project is estimated at 2.5 million Euros. The acronym GEC stands for Gravitational wave Electromagnetic Calorimeter.

. While Artificial Intelligence (AI) has significantly advanced our capacity to acquire information, it has simultaneously enabled deception and misinformation dissemination. Consequently, there is an urgent need for Explainable AI (XAI) systems capable of delivering truthful insights while ensuring transparency. This paper introduces a novel framework designed to facilitate truthful knowledge dissemination through AI by integrating XAI principles. We demonstrate that integrating XAI allows the system to function as a verifiable oracle, thereby enabling genuine knowledge dissemination. Furthermore, we illustrate that this approach supports the creation of intelligent agents that can derive new insights by leveraging this verifiable knowledge. As a practical application, we present a prototype that utilizes a digital library of such agents to offer personalized recommendations for learning new skills. Empirical evaluations confirm that this prototype effectively imparts knowledge and provides accurate recommendations. Additionally, we show that the system can identify and exclude deceptive insights, thereby enhancing its ability to learn truthful information. To our knowledge, this is the first research to prove that AI can both disseminate and acquire truthful knowledge. The source code and prototypes are available at https://github.com/rohanrathod/TKE.

Artificial Intelligence (AI) has enabled the creation of sophisticated models that derive insights from vast datasets; however, this capability also opens avenues for generating deceptive insights. This work proposes that AI can function as a verifiable oracle to disseminate truthful knowledge, allowing other AI agents to acquire this knowledge and subsequently produce truthful insights. We introduce the concept of Truthful Knowledge Empowerment (TKE), which encompasses methods for creating a digital library of agents empowered with truthful knowledge. As a demonstration, we developed a prototype that provides personalized recommendations for learning new skills. Our findings indicate that TKE successfully eliminates the risk of deceptive recommendations and empowers the system to learn truthful knowledge, even when the underlying AI models are prone to deception.

We also present a prototype that offers personalized recommendations for learning new skills, demonstrating its capacity to avoid deceptive suggestions and learn truthful knowledge.

This lack of interpretability hinders the deployment of NLP in high-stakes domains like healthcare and law, where understanding model behavior is essential. Furthermore, without interpretability, detecting and correcting flaws in NLP models becomes a challenging task. This paper introduces a new framework designed to enhance the diagnosis of errors in neural machine translation (NMT) by leveraging counterfactual analysis. Our method generates counterfactual inputs and outputs, offering explanations for both correct and incorrect translations. Additionally, we utilize these counterfactuals to identify specific areas within source sentences that cause NMT errors. We validate our approach on two distinct NMT tasks: cross-lingual morphological handling and English-to-Chinese translation. Empirical results demonstrate that our method produces informative explanations and effectively locates error-causing regions, thereby successfully advancing the goals of NLP diagnosis and interpretability.

This formulation faces significant challenges, particularly in theories with multiple gauge fields where the validity of the conjecture would depend on an unphysical choice of gauge. To address this, we propose a formulation of the Weak Gravity Conjecture applicable to theories involving several gauge fields that is both physical and robust. Our approach relies on analyzing the decay of the heaviest particle within the framework of the positive mass conjecture. We demonstrate that this method successfully recovers the standard conjecture in single gauge field scenarios and establishes a novel statement for multi-gauge field contexts. Furthermore, we contend that this formulation is more pertinent to the study of swamplands than its traditional counterpart. As an illustration, we provide a concrete example showing how our version of the conjecture excludes the specific window of effective field theories associated with large extra dimensions. Additionally, we present a formulation that avoids the ambiguities arising from the mass gap problem. In this context, we argue that the necessary adjustments are minimal and that our core methodology remains applicable. Ultimately, our formulation offers a physically meaningful and robust statement of the Weak Gravity Conjecture for multi-gauge field theories, a goal that has been lacking until now.
In this paper, we examine the renormalization group (RG) flow of the $O(N)$ Gross-Neveu model in $d=2$ dimensions, specifically focusing on the behavior of the $N/N_c$ ratio, where $N_c$ represents the number of colors. We determine the exact value of this ratio at the infrared fixed point using two distinct approaches. First, we calculate the two-loop anomalous dimension of the bilinear operator and apply the unitarity bound to derive the corresponding ratio. Second, we employ the matrix model method, which involves summing planar diagrams, to compute the two-loop free energy and subsequently extract the required ratio. Our findings indicate that $N/N_c=2.25$. This result aligns with the prediction from AdS/CFT correspondence for the same parameter and confirms the existence of an isolated fixed point, thereby supporting the Necessity Conjecture.

Specifically, we demonstrate that applying the inverse of a general unitary operator, $U^\dagger_\theta = e^{i\theta U}$, necessitates adding $U^\dagger_\theta P$ to the Hamiltonian for each unitary gate $P$ within the Hamiltonian's decomposition, where $P$ is Hermitian. Consequently, the required number of measurements per Hamiltonian term scales exponentially with the number of qubits for general Hamiltonians, rendering the method impractical for even modestly sized systems. To overcome this challenge, we derive that applying the imaginary time evolution operator $e^{-H\tau}$ to a quantum state is equivalent to evolving the state and the Hamiltonian simultaneously under the same Schrödinger evolution. This insight forms the basis of our proposed "model-space QITE" method. Within this approach, a variational quantum computer efficiently measures the system Hamiltonian, while a classical computer updates the Hamiltonian according to the desired evolution. We validate this technique numerically using both exact diagonalization and a quantum approximate optimization algorithm (QAOA) as model spaces. Results indicate that our method achieves convergence to the target ground state with significantly fewer evolution steps compared to single-time-step QITE. Furthermore, the method exhibits high robustness against measurement errors and does not depend on the specific form of the Hamiltonian decomposition, offering substantial advantages for applications involving Hamiltonians that are difficult to implement on quantum devices. This work establishes a straightforward yet potent strategy for applying general time-evolution operators to quantum systems.

novel approaches for modeling and simulating power systems. The AC Power Flow Equilibrium Problem (ACPF) serves as a fundamental tool for analyzing the steady-state behavior of electrical networks. This paper introduces a new Mixed Integer Nonlinear Programming (MINLP) formulation of the ACPF, which is solved using the open-source algorithms BONMIN and ANTGP. These algorithms employ the Generalized Benders Decomposition (GBD) framework, enhanced by strong feasibility cuts to accelerate the search for global optima. Formulating the ACPF as a MINLP enables the application of powerful global optimization techniques to power flow analysis. The study validates this approach through a numerical case study involving the IEEE 14-bus test system. Additionally, the authors provide an open-source implementation of their algorithm and solvers, accessible at https://github.com/ahmedhassan20/ACPF-MINLP. This work also presents a new MINLP formulation of the ACPF and demonstrates that GBD effectively solves this formulation to global optimality. The proposed algorithm outperforms existing state-of-the-art methods for solving MINLPs. Furthermore, the algorithm's performance is benchmarked against popular solvers designed specifically for the ACPF.

The primary objective of this research is to develop a method for assessing the security of DC transmission lines against single contingencies. The proposed approach utilizes the DC Optimal Power Flow (DCOPF) formulation to calculate line flow margins under base operating conditions and across all possible contingency scenarios. These margins are then employed to determine the security status of each transmission line. The proposed method offers two key advantages: it is computationally efficient and capable of handling transmission lines with series capacitors. The approach is validated using the IEEE 118-bus test system.

This paper proposes a unified framework for solving the AC Optimal Power Flow (ACOPF) problem that integrates interior-point methods with Generalized Benders Decomposition (GBD). This decomposition is essential for guaranteeing global optimality in non-convex problems. By exploiting the duality gap between the primal ACOPF and its DC approximation, the framework employs strong duality cuts to achieve a solution rate superior to existing GBD-based methods for the ACOPF. The approach is applicable to both transmission and distribution networks. Validation is performed on the IEEE 14-bus and IEEE 30-bus test systems.
