In this work, we examine the distribution of diameters across all possible sets $S$ for a fixed group $G$. Specifically, we define $N_G(k)$ as the count of sets $S$ for which $diam(G,S)$ equals $k$, and $p_G(k)$ as the probability that a randomly selected set $S$ yields a diameter of $k$. Our main finding demonstrates that for any finite group $G$, the diameter is typically small when $S$ is chosen at random; more formally, if $p_G(k)$ denotes this probability, then $p_G(k) \ll 1/k$. This result is derived by analyzing the distribution of lengths within the ball of radius $k$ in Cayley graphs. As an application, we prove that for any finite group $G$ and any $\epsilon > 0$, there exists a threshold $k_0$ such that for all $k \ge k_0$, the number of symmetric generating sets with diameter at most $k$ is at least $(1-\epsilon) times the total number of symmetric generating sets. Furthermore, we provide an explicit lower bound for the diameter of sets chosen at random from a finite group $G$. Finally, we investigate the distribution of diameters for finite simple groups in detail, determining precise values for $N_G(k)$ and $p_G(k)$ in certain cases. In particular, we show that if a finite simple group $G$ of order greater than $200$ is selected at random and equipped with a randomly chosen set of generators, the probability that the resulting diameter is at least $100$ exceeds $0.999$. Additionally, we note that the methods employed in this paper can be utilized to address other questions regarding the distribution of diameters in random subgraphs of a group.

Introduction

This review provides an accessible overview of the functional renormalization group (FRG) and recent findings regarding its use in QCD. While a comprehensive treatment of both theoretical foundations and recent advancements would exceed the scope of this paper, our primary objective is to present the FRG approach alongside its recent successes in a clear manner. As a companion to [1], this review is designed for a broad audience, including researchers in quantum gravity, statistical field theory, and nuclear physics.

Section II outlines the foundational principles of the FRG, beginning with an overview of renormalization in quantum field theory (QFT). It then details the two equivalent formulations of the FRG: the Polchinski equation and the Wetterich equation. These formulations are shown to be equivalent to standard effective actions derived through integrating out high-energy modes. Section III demonstrates how these methods can be employed to track the evolution of the QCD beta function and quark anomalous dimensions from the infrared to the ultraviolet regimes. In Section IV, we introduce two distinct regularized QCD actions that permit the determination of the renormalization group flow of coupling constants via the FRG. Section V presents the central contribution of this review: an extensive discussion of recent FRG studies on QCD phase transitions. Specifically, we explore the phase diagram of quark matter, with a particular focus on the nature of the transition between the color-superconducting and deconfined phases. In Section VI, we summarize the conclusions drawn in this review and in [1].

Throughout this work, we utilize natural units where $\hbar=c=k_{\rm B}=1$.

A promising strategy involves searching for UHECRs that deviate from Lorentz invariance, as their trajectories would be altered by quantum gravity effects, enabling us to trace them back to their origins. This study examines the feasibility of this approach by modeling the propagation of UHECRs through the Milky Way. We simulate proton and iron UHECRs traveling from the Galactic Center to the Solar System under various Lorentz-symmetry-breaking scenarios. Our propagation models, which incorporate both quantum gravity effects and standard astrophysical influences, reveal that these effects are substantial. Specifically, we observe that flavor-changing interactions between protons and electrons within the Galactic disk can mimic the impact of quantum gravity, while the deflection of iron nuclei by the Galactic magnetic field can fully reproduce the signatures of Lorentz violation. These findings suggest that, to effectively utilize UHECRs as origin tracers in the presence of Lorentz symmetry breaking, one must account for propagation effects within our Galaxy. Furthermore, we demonstrate that astrophysical processes can fully replicate the anomalies reported in recent UHECR data, thereby offering a viable explanation for the excess of electrons and muons detected by the Pierre Auger Observatory. Finally, we conclude that the arrival directions of UHECRs can serve as a robust test for distinguishing between quantum gravity-induced deflection and magnetic deflection. This study employs a network model of branched polymers to examine how the extension of network strands during flow impacts the shear thickening observed in entangled systems. We introduce a new parameter, $\xi_{\rm ext}$, which quantifies the degree of strand extension and correlates with the lengthening of polymer chains. The competition's goal is to identify and remove spurious correlations in training data that cause an algorithm to make incorrect predictions on test samples. We approached this by formulating it as a novel optimization problem, which we detail in this document. While our primary focus was on algorithms requiring minimal human input, we also explore additional methods that require little to no post-hoc adjustment.

We detail a methodology that leverages extensive human analysis to identify and eliminate spurious correlations within training data, ensuring models do not rely on them. Specifically, we present a custom optimization framework that reformulates the challenge into a mixed-integer linear program (MILP), solved using a branch-and-cut algorithm. Additionally, we introduce a novel, fully automatic approach that achieves comparable results with significantly lower computational cost.

Our proposed methodology consists of two primary components. First, we present a method requiring substantial human involvement to identify spurious correlations, followed by a custom algorithm designed to enforce their absence in predictions. Second, we detail a fully automatic approach that achieves comparable performance with significantly reduced computational overhead. Our custom algorithm comprises three key stages: (1) an analysis phase to determine the number of clusters ($K$) and the assignment of training examples to clusters; (2) a reformulation of the original optimization problem as a MILP, where $K$ represents the maximum number of clusters and $x_{i,j}$ indicates whether example $i$ belongs to cluster $j$; and (3) the execution of a branch-and-cut algorithm to solve this problem.

Our automatic method is grounded in the observation that the core challenge lies in eliminating correlations between features and labels that are not present across the entire dataset. We achieve this by learning a low-dimensional representation of the data that captures only these global correlations. Our approach utilizes a variant of contrastive learning, where pairs of examples sharing the same label are pulled closer together in the latent space, while pairs with different labels are pushed apart. This technique effectively removes local spurious correlations.

In our analysis, we demonstrate that the competition's evaluation metric can be expressed as a function of cluster assignments, allowing us to optimize it directly. We show that optimizing this metric is mathematically equivalent to the competition's specified optimization problem. Furthermore, we detail how to solve this formulation using a branch-and-bound approach, which aligns with the techniques employed in the track 1 (unsupervised learning)

Within the Hele-Shaw approximation, we derive a generalized dispersion relation applicable to both scenarios. Our analysis reveals that in the presence of surface tension, the instability remains conservative, characterized by a neutral curve that separates stable from stable states. Conversely, when the interface follows a prescribed viscosity ratio, the instability becomes dissipative, with the neutral curve defining a stable interior. These theoretical predictions are validated through direct numerical simulations of a finger advancing into the medium. Furthermore, we demonstrate that the instability is dissipative regardless of whether the flow is confined between parallel plates or occurs within a single porous layer. Finally, we show that the nature of the instability—whether conservative or dissipative—remains consistent for both steady and time-periodic flows. These findings offer a comprehensive understanding of the instability dynamics in Hele-Shaw flows involving a viscous fluid invading another fluid of the same viscosity.

The movement of fluids within porous media is critical in various natural and industrial processes, such as groundwater contamination, oil and gas extraction, carbon dioxide sequestration, and the separation of fluids from solids. This phenomenon is frequently modeled using the Hele-Shaw approximation, which applies to both single porous layers and gaps between two parallel plates. In these configurations, the flow is typically dominated by viscous forces, rendering the Reynolds number negligible. Additionally, the flow is often constrained by a dominant surface tension term, quantified by a small Weber number. Under these conditions, the Navier-Stokes equations simplify to the Darcy equations within the porous medium and the biharmonic equation for the stream function in the Hele-Shaw channel.

In Hele-Shaw flows involving a fluid displacing another of the same viscosity, the dominant physics is driven by either viscosity or surface tension. When surface tension is significant, the problem is often reformulated as a free boundary problem where the interface is determined by a prescribed viscosity ratio. This approach has been applied to analyze the instability of a fluid finger penetrating a porous medium, as well as the instability of a fluid front advancing into such a medium. Previous research has explored the instability of a fluid finger in a Hele-Shaw channel filled with another fluid, identifying that when surface tension is present, the instability is conservative, whereas it is dissipative when governed by a viscosity ratio. Specifically, we utilize this method to analyze the structural relaxation of a polymeric liquid, the glycerol-based glass former Glycerol-Gly, across a wide temperature range spanning from the glass transition to the bulk melting point. By examining the evolution of the underlying microstate distribution, we identify two distinct relaxation regimes: cooperative and cage. This paper introduces a novel attention mechanism designed for NMT that employs a unidirectional approach combined with context-based residual attention. By leveraging learned residual attention maps, the model captures long-distance dependencies through the standard self-attention mechanism within a forward-only framework. Additionally, the model filters out redundant forward attention by identifying words with similar contexts. Experiments conducted on the WMT 2014 English-to-German dataset demonstrate that the proposed model achieves a new state-of-the-art BLEU score of 28.6, surpassing the baseline by 1.2 BLEU points. Furthermore, attention analysis reveals that the proposed mechanism effectively learns meaningful attention maps. The model's implementation and evaluation code are available at https://github.com/zhengyuanz/UniResAttention.

Machine translation aims to map a source sentence to its corresponding target translation. While sequence-to-sequence models have demonstrated remarkable success, they often suffer from a vocabulary mismatch problem, where many target words are not present in the source vocabulary. Although multi-target attention has been proposed to mitigate this issue, it requires further investigation. This study offers a comprehensive analysis of attention mechanisms in neural machine translation. We identify three primary limitations: (1) models frequently assign excessive weight to a few source tokens, (2) there is a mismatch between source and target attention distributions, and (3) there is a discrepancy between the target vocabulary and the set of source tokens receiving non-zero attention. Based on these findings, we introduce multi-target attention, which explicitly models these mismatches. Additionally, we propose a new mechanism called multi-target disentangled attention, which utilizes a projection matrix to learn this mapping. This approach enhances translation quality for out-of-vocabulary words and improves overall translation accuracy. Experiments on the WMT 2014 English-to-German dataset confirm that our method outperforms standard multi-source attention by 1.5 BLEU points.

Machine translation systems often assign disproportionately high attention to a limited number of source tokens, a phenomenon known as excessive attention. This behavior can lead to poor translations for out-of-vocabulary words. This paper investigates the causes of excessive attention and proposes a novel mechanism, Multi-Head Disproportionate Attention (MDA), to mitigate it. To achieve this, researchers are increasingly leveraging the computational power of high-performance computing (HPC) systems. However, the substantial energy consumption of HPC has prompted the exploration of energy-efficient alternatives, with federated learning (FL) emerging as a promising solution. This paper introduces a novel framework for energy-aware FL on HPC, designed to minimize energy usage while maintaining high training accuracy. The framework incorporates an adaptive batch size strategy that adjusts batch dimensions based on the energy profiles of participating nodes and an adaptive learning rate mechanism that utilizes a reward system to enhance learning efficiency. Experimental results demonstrate that this approach effectively reduces energy consumption across diverse FL scenarios. Additionally, the framework has been implemented as an open-source tool named Energy-Aware Federated Learning on High-Performance Computing (EAFHPC). This implementation serves as a resource for the research community to advance energy-aware FL on HPC and supports the broader translational genomics initiative. The EAFHPC framework is accessible at https://github.com/rajkumar007/EAFHPC.

Federated learning (FL) has gained significant traction in recent years, particularly in healthcare, due to its ability to train models on distributed data without compromising patient privacy. Despite the privacy benefits of keeping data local, the computational demands of FL can be substantial. This study examines the computational requirements of FL algorithms, focusing on the impact of data dimensionality and volume. We conducted experiments using the Federated Averaging (FedAvg) algorithm across various datasets, including MNIST, Fashion-MNIST, and CIFAR-10, to evaluate the energy consumption of FL. Our findings indicate that FL consumes between 1.5 and 2.5 times more energy than traditional centralized machine learning training. To address this issue, we developed a method to reduce energy consumption by optimizing the number of training epochs. Experimental results confirm that this proposed method is effective in lowering the energy usage of FL.

This model is characterized by a single non-minimal coupling parameter, $\xi$, which governs interactions between these components and the spacetime metric. Notably, the model successfully recovers the standard $\Lambda$CDM scenario as a limiting case when $\xi = 0$. Through rigorous numerical analysis, we demonstrate that $\xi$ can be constrained to the narrow interval $[-0.0001, 0.0001]$ by combining data from cosmic microwave background (CMB) anisotropies and the expansion history of the universe. This result indicates that the proposed dark fluid model is highly consistent with the well-established $\Lambda$CDM model. Furthermore, we find that the model remains viable even when the Hubble tension is included in the analysis, provided that a CMB-based Hubble constant measurement is excluded. Additionally, the model offers a potential explanation for the recently reported detection of neutrino oscillations on cosmological scales. A key advantage of this approach is its simplicity, relying on only one free parameter beyond the standard cosmological model. Finally, we conclude with a discussion of the model's implications for future investigations.

While numerous models have been developed to mimic this trait, they often operate in isolation, failing to account for the complex interplay between different facets of curiosity. This study introduces a unified framework designed to simulate that interaction. The model incorporates three distinct mechanisms, each representing a specific dimension of curiosity: knowledge-driven exploration, active inference, and meta-cognitive exploration. Validation across various scenarios demonstrates that these mechanisms effectively replicate behaviors observed in real subjects. Furthermore, the model demonstrates superior performance in balancing exploration and exploitation compared to existing state-of-the-art approaches. These findings offer valuable insights for enhancing artificial curiosity within advanced autonomous systems.

Artificial curiosity is a key component for creating versatile and proactive agents capable of functioning in dynamic, real-world settings. This paper presents a novel framework that integrates multiple curiosity mechanisms to enable agents to engage with their surroundings more meaningfully. We implement three mechanisms: knowledge-driven exploration, active inference, and meta-cognitive exploration. Our implementation utilizes the Point Cloud Deep Q-Network (PCDQN) algorithm for knowledge-driven behavior, adapting it to process raw 3D data. The active inference mechanism is built upon the work of Friston and Shaliastovich. Additionally, we designed a mechanism to encourage the agent to visit locations it has rarely or never visited. Extensive experiments show that this framework significantly improves the agent's performance in both simulation and real-world environments.

This work investigates the application of active inference as a model of artificial curiosity. We achieve this by implementing two mechanisms: one that drives the agent to seek new knowledge and another that promotes the exploration of novel states. These mechanisms are grounded in the concepts of surprise minimization and entropy maximization, respectively. To demonstrate the utility of our approach, we implemented it within a reinforcement learning framework and tested it across various simulation tasks. The results indicate that our mechanism successfully encourages the agent to explore new environments and acquire new skills.

Curiosity is a multifaceted trait that motivates agents to interact with and learn from their environments. This paper implements two mechanisms to drive an agent's behavior: one that encourages the pursuit of new information and another that drives the visitation of novel states. We employ value prediction and novelty prediction to calculate informational and intrinsic values, respectively. These valuations guide the agent's behavior through temporal difference learning. We tested our implementation in both simulation and real-world settings, and the results confirm that our mechanism successfully drives the agent to explore new states and learn from its surroundings.

While numerous Gaussian process models exist, many rely on covariance kernels that are computationally expensive, particularly for high-dimensional data. This paper introduces a novel class of periodic Gaussian processes that utilizes a low-rank, computationally efficient kernel. Learning the relationship between inputs and outputs is fundamental to data science, yet it remains challenging when data is scarce, noisy, or high-dimensional. Gaussian processes are widely recognized for their ability to model unknown functions by defining probabilistic priors on inputs and outputs. However, many standard Gaussian process kernels are computationally demanding, a limitation that becomes critical in high-dimensional settings. This work presents a new family of periodic kernels designed to be computationally tractable and low-rank. We show that variational inference can be effectively applied to this proposed kernel, supported by both theoretical analysis and practical implementation. Validated against multiple high-dimensional periodic datasets, our findings indicate that this new Gaussian process significantly outperforms current state-of-the-art methods. The implementation can be found at https://github.com/AmirHosseinKarami/Periodic-Gaussian-Process.

Gaussian processes are a powerful tool for regression and function learning, offering probabilistic predictions alongside uncertainty estimates. Despite these advantages, their reliance on covariance kernels often results in high computational costs, which is especially problematic in high-dimensional contexts. This paper proposes a new family of periodic kernels that are both computationally efficient and low-rank. We provide both theoretical and practical frameworks for applying variational inference to this new kernel. Our results demonstrate that this approach outperforms state-of-the-art techniques across several high-dimensional periodic datasets. The code is accessible at https://github.com/AmirHosseinKarami/Periodic-Gaussian-Process.

of urban mobility systems. While automated systems using cameras and sensors are common, they are often too costly for widespread deployment. Consequently, road users are increasingly encouraged to contribute to data collection via participatory sensing. This study examines a scenario where drivers within a city voluntarily share their locations to identify and map all road segments they traverse. We analyze the relationship between the proportion of participating users and the proportion of correctly mapped road segments. Specifically, we introduce a novel analytical model that calculates the probability of a road segment being mapped based on the density of potential participants. Validated through both analytical methods and simulations, this approach offers a more precise assessment of participatory sensing potential for road mapping than previous studies. The findings are particularly relevant for assessing the viability of in-vehicle sensing systems designed to map road networks. The open-source code for this research is available at https://github.com/AmirHosseinD/Mapping-Road-Networks-via-Participatory-Sensing.

Urban road networks are critical for the smooth operation of city mobility, and monitoring them is fundamental to maintaining this functionality. Although automated monitoring using cameras and sensors is a prevalent solution, its high cost limits deployment to specific areas. Therefore, there is growing interest in utilizing mobile sensing via road users to gather additional data. This paper focuses on a scenario where a city's road network is mapped by drivers who voluntarily share their GPS locations. We derive an analytical formula to determine the probability that a specific road segment is mapped, given the density of potential participants. This probability is influenced by the orientation of the road relative to the participant density and the sensing accuracy of the in-vehicle system. The proposed model was validated against simulations and further tested using real-world data from a city in Iran. The analytical approach yields more accurate results regarding the potential of participatory sensing for road mapping compared to existing literature. This methodology can also be adapted to assess the potential of such systems for other sensing tasks. The code for this research is accessible at https://github.com/AmirHosseinD/Mapping-Road-Networks-via-Participatory-Sensing.

While previous attempts to adapt Riemannian time series analysis for missing data relied on embedding these series into Euclidean spaces, our approach retains the Riemannian structure throughout the methodology. We demonstrate that MFSSA is equivalent to applying Euclidean SSA to the tangent space of a specific Euclidean Jordan algebra, which provides a theoretical foundation for preserving geometric properties during the analysis of functional time series on manifolds. The utility of MFSSA is illustrated through an application to daily temperature data on a circle, which effectively reveals a seasonal pattern and outperforms existing methods in a simulation study. While these systems offer the potential for human-like feedback at scale, they often lack transparency regarding the origins of their predictions. This study investigates the reliability of a popular AES system by analyzing its responses to thousands of real human-graded essays and synthetic data. Our findings indicate that the system frequently produces unreliable scores, particularly for low-quality essays where minor variations in language can lead to significant score fluctuations. Furthermore, we observe that the system exhibits an over-reliance on specific words and phrases, a tendency that often diverges from human scoring criteria. Based on these insights, we propose several strategies to enhance the system's reliability. Ultimately, this research underscores the necessity of validating AES systems against human standards before deployment and calls for future development of more reliable automated scoring technologies.

This research details a novel method for measuring the IEDF using a Langmuir probe, achieved by synchronizing the mechanical movement of the probe with its insertion into and extraction from the plasma. This approach allows for the acquisition of one-dimensional IEDF data across a full range of distances from the target wall. The resulting profiles are analyzed using a theoretical model to derive the floating potential, plasma density, and ion temperature. Validation of these findings is performed through a comparison with IEDF data obtained from a view-screen camera. The study also examines the influence of plasma flow velocity on the extraction of IEDF information and evaluates the method's applicability under varying magnetic field strengths. Furthermore, the technique's utility in measuring the velocity of ion acoustic waves is explored. Ultimately, this proposed method offers a straightforward and effective means of obtaining IEDF data at multiple points within the IShTAR facility. Additionally, it paves the way for future enhancements, such as integrating a multi-channel oscilloscope to capture time-resolved IEDF data from multiple locations simultaneously. These improvements would facilitate the determination of ion acoustic wave velocity and the analysis of wave propagation patterns.

Plasma-wall interactions are critical in the operation of Radio Frequency (RF) heliostats, which direct ion beams onto the first wall of the ITER divertor. To investigate these interactions, the IShTAR facility at the FOM Institute for Plasma Physics (KIT) in the Netherlands is being upgraded. A new target chamber has been installed, featuring a movable multi-diagnostic view screen and a multi-channel Langmuir probe system. This new setup enables the measurement of ion energy distribution functions (IEDF) at multiple positions within the main volume of the chamber. The primary objective of this paper is to demonstrate the capability of this new Langmuir probe system to measure the IEDF at various locations within the target chamber. The system was calibrated to ensure accurate IEDF measurements across a broad spectrum of plasma conditions. To validate the system's performance, it was tested in the RF plasma source of IShTAR, where its data was compared against a single Langmuir probe and a view-screen camera. adverse impacts associated with chemical pesticides. However, the susceptibility of these biocontrol agents to environmental stressors remains a significant challenge. This study examines the effects of the antifungal agent amphotericin B (AmB) on the entomopathogenic fungus *Metarhizium anisopliae*. The research demonstrates that AmB is toxic to *M. anisopliae*, inhibiting both mycelial growth and conidial germination in a dose-dependent manner. Furthermore, electron microscopy analysis revealed that AmB treatment causes severe ultrastructural damage to the fungal cells of *M. anisopliae*. Additionally, the study found that AmB disrupts the antioxidant defense system in *M. anisopliae*, leading to oxidative stress. This damage is evidenced by the accumulation of reactive oxygen species (ROS), the depletion of glutathione (GSH), and the depletion of key antioxidant enzymes such as superoxide dismutase (SOD), catalase (CAT), and glutathione reductase (GR). Ultimately, this research indicates that oxidative stress is a primary mechanism driving the antifungal activity of AmB against *M. anisopliae*. These findings provide a theoretical basis for understanding the sensitivity of *M. anisopliae* to AmB and suggest that this knowledge could inform the development of more effective microbial pesticides. Additionally, the data may support the creation of strategies to mitigate the resistance of target pests to *M. anisopliae*.

However, these models often fail in real-world applications due to domain shifts caused by variations in staining, imaging equipment, and data collection protocols. To address this, domain adaptation techniques have been introduced to enhance generalization across different domains. This paper investigates the rationality over $\Q(i)$ of the special values at $s=\frac{1}{2}+n$ for both the twisted Gamma function $\Gamma_\chi(s)$ and the twisted Bessel function $\Omega_\chi(s)$, where $n\in\Z_{\geq 0}$ and $\Gamma_\chi(s)=\Gamma(s,\Psi,\chi)=\int_{F^\times}\Psi(1/2|x|)\chi(x)ds$. The analysis relies on integral expressions for the derivatives at $s=\frac{1}{2}+n$ of the twisted Gamma function, utilizing the higher local Bessel numbers introduced by K. Bringmann and K. Ono. Specifically, when $n$ is odd, the $n$-th derivative of $\Gamma_\chi(s)$ at $s=\frac{1}{2}$ is expressed as a linear combination of integrals involving the twisted Bessel function $\Omega_\chi(s)$, with coefficients in $\Q(i)$. The study further examines the rationality of these integrals, covering all cases where $\chi$ is a quadratic character and specific cases for non-quadratic $\chi$. Notably, if $\chi$ is non-quadratic, it is proven that at least one of the integrals of $\Omega_\chi(s)$ at $s=0$ or $s=1$ fails to be rational. In this study, we investigate the ill-posedness of this system within the 3D framework established by Xiong and Liu. Specifically, we show that if magnetic dissipation is absent, the system exhibits Sobolev ill-posedness. Furthermore, even with partial magnetic dissipation, the system remains ill-posed for small initial data. These findings highlight the significant impact of anisotropy on the dynamics of MHD equations. Additionally, we provide improved lower bounds for the lifespan of strong solutions to the anisotropic MHD system with partial magnetic dissipation. While the NLRP3 inflammasome is a primary driver of this process, the specific upstream signals required to activate it remain unclear. This study demonstrates that the kinase JNK can directly bind to and phosphorylate NLRP3, thereby activating the inflammasome and inducing pyroptosis in response to viral infections. In cell culture models, both JNK inhibitors and siRNA-mediated silencing of JNK prevented NLRP3 inflammasome activation and subsequent pyroptosis caused by various viruses. Similarly, blocking JNK activity using small molecule inhibitors or viral proteases during infection led to reduced viral replication and increased cell survival. Furthermore, in a mouse model of influenza A virus infection, pharmacological inhibition of JNK significantly lowered viral loads in the lungs and enhanced host survival. These findings reveal that the direct interaction and phosphorylation of NLRP3 by JNK constitute a critical pathway for inflammasome activation and pyroptosis during viral challenges. The research also suggests that disrupting the JNK-NLRP3 axis represents a promising therapeutic strategy for mitigating viral pathogenicity.

While prior research has primarily analyzed the impact of a single exogenous variable, this paper investigates multiple such variables and their induced Markovian dynamics. We introduce a simplified learning task and reveal a counterintuitive finding: a variable offering superior reward signals may be more detrimental than one providing minimal information. To address this, we develop a theoretical framework for evaluating the utility of exogenous variables within a multi-agent setting. This framework characterizes the difficulty of learning the environment's transition model and highlights a counterintuitive optimal scenario where no exogenous variables are present. Finally, we validate these findings through an extensive empirical study on various gridworlds, demonstrating significant gaps between the learned and true transition models when relevant exogenous variables are included. These results underscore the critical nature of spurious correlations in reinforcement learning and suggest that adding informative reward signals can exacerbate the problem.

Exogenous state variables can both help and hurt reinforcement learning. Previous work has mostly focused on their potential to cause harm, yet under specific conditions, they can actually facilitate learning. We examine a scenario where an exogenous variable provides more information about the reward, making it harder for an agent to learn the underlying dynamics, than a variable that reveals very little. We propose a framework for assessing the informativeness of these variables and show that, in certain cases, it is optimal to have none at all. Our experimental results confirm these counterintuitive findings.

Reinforcement learning algorithms can struggle when a state variable is informative regarding the reward but not the transition dynamics. We explore a setting where the reward signal's quality depends on an exogenous variable, either revealing whether the agent received a positive signal or how strong it was. We demonstrate that if the variable is highly informative about the rewards, an agent may find it more difficult to learn the transition dynamics compared to when the variable is largely uninformative. We also present a theoretical framework for analyzing the difficulty of learning transition dynamics in the presence of exogenous variables. This analysis reveals that, in a simplified task, the optimal exogenous variable is one that provides the least amount of information. These theoretical insights are supported by experiments in gridworld environments.

Blockchains enable decentralized applications and provide a trusted environment for processing transactions. However, the potential for errors in these systems is substantial, and the industry currently lacks effective methods to identify bugs. Solidity, the primary programming language for modern blockchains like Ethereum, offers powerful features to enhance application capabilities, yet these same features complicate bug detection. Existing static analysis tools often yield numerous false positives, hindering the identification of genuine bugs. This paper introduces a Soot-based translator that converts Solidity code into Java byte code, enabling the application of existing Java analysis tools to Solidity programs. We demonstrate the practical utility of this translator by integrating it with two existing tools: one for determining function equivalence and another for detecting buffer overflows. Furthermore, we show that the translator can be extended to identify specific bugs inherent to Solidity, such as unexpected integer overflows.

The proliferation of smart contracts has led to a surge in automated testing tools, yet there remains a scarcity of static analysis solutions. We propose a translator capable of converting Solidity code into Java byte code, a format supported by mature static analysis tools. This translator is intended to assist in identifying bugs that current specialized analyzers miss. Our evaluation reveals that the translator successfully detects bugs found by state-of-the-art smart contract analyzers, as well as additional vulnerabilities specific to Solidity that those tools cannot find.

# Introduction

Graph Convolutional Neural Networks (GCNNs) were first introduced to enable graph-based learning tasks, such as node and graph classification, and have since been successfully applied to diverse problems involving data with interconnections, including social networks, transportation systems, and biological networks. Despite these advancements, GCNNs remain a relatively recent development within the field of graph-based optimization.

In many real-world applications, data naturally forms a graph structure, and the associated tasks often involve high-dimensional data that is computationally prohibitive to solve directly. For instance, in machine learning, the goal is typically to train a model by optimizing an objective function over a loss derived from a dataset. When the dataset is extensive, it is more practical to represent the data as a graph and optimize using a smaller subset. Similarly, in control theory, one may seek to optimize the trajectories of numerous interconnected agents, where the resulting objective functions are high-dimensional.

To address such challenges, researchers have recently developed Graph Neural Networks for Optimization (GNN4O), a class of algorithms that combine graph-based message-passing techniques with iterative first- and second-order optimization methods. These algorithms are particularly effective for large-scale convex optimization, offering superior performance compared to traditional approaches when the number of data points is high.

Although deep learning has been applied to elastography for automated lesion segmentation and classification, the method is not yet standard clinical practice. Consequently, there is a critical need to investigate how these deep learning models perform when encountering out-of-distribution (OOD) data. This study specifically examines a common OOD scenario: lesions with shapes and sizes that differ from those in the training set. We evaluated a deep learning network designed for both segmentation and classification using a dataset of breast lesions that varies in shape and size. This method involves training a deep learning network on RF data to predict the maximum displacement map, which is then applied to the elastography image for elastogram generation. Experimental findings indicate that this approach yields a 10% improvement in segmentation accuracy and a 5% boost in classification accuracy for OOD lesions. By utilizing readily available high-frequency RF data, this method offers a promising solution for enhancing the diagnosis of breast lesions with atypical shapes and sizes.

These structures correspond directly to Gentzen's "natural deduction" style of proofs. We demonstrate that natural deduction trees are in bijective correspondence with "sequent calculus trees," which represent sequent calculus proofs and also generate correct programs through the use of a specific operational semantics. Furthermore, the application of specific transformation rules converts any sequent calculus tree into an equivalent natural deduction tree, a process that preserves computational behavior. Consequently, natural deduction trees offer a robust representation of proofs that ensures the correctness of generated programs. This work elucidates the relationship between these two systems of formal logic and underscores their significance in programming languages. Specifically, it reveals that there exists a one-to-one mapping between "equivalence classes of proofs" and "equivalence classes of programs," where this correspondence is established via a pair of inverse functions. Notably, this relationship holds true even when the underlying type theory is undecidable. To achieve this, we define the interpretation of programs within a denotational semantics framework based on domain theory. This approach facilitates a bijective relationship between programs and proofs, thereby proving program correctness. Additionally, we explore the correspondence between programs and "refined types," which are defined as first-order logical formulas. Refined types provide precise specifications of program properties, and this mapping remains valid regardless of whether type checking is decidable. The central contributions of this work are the development of natural deduction trees and the revelation of their profound connection to Hoare's triplets. The former represents correct programs with verified correctness proofs, while the latter specify the refined types of those programs. The proposed methodology for proving program correctness is grounded in the equivalence between natural deduction trees and Hoare triplets.

The significance of proofs and programs is deeply rooted in the Curry-Howard correspondence, which establishes a fundamental link between type theory and logic. This relationship is essential for developing correct programs, a goal that has been pursued for decades. The work of Per Martin-Löf and J. Roger Hindley laid the groundwork for creating programming languages capable of generating and verifying correct programs. Their insights enabled the formulation of a type system that supports a static analysis for ensuring correctness. This system allows for the specification of program properties through "refined types," where the type of an expression can be deduced based on its structure. This capability is crucial for verifying programs, as it enables the use of automated tools to confirm that the specified properties hold true

we examine the probability of winning in a race between two players, Alice and Bob, where their relative performance is governed by a Markov chain. We derive an explicit formula for the win probability as a function of the players' current relative standing and the race's leading position. Our findings reveal that the advantage of a trailing participant diminishes as the number of items increases; specifically, in a race involving real numbers, the winner is determined by the item currently in the lead. Additionally, we explore the implications of these results for the classic problem of determining the optimal strategy to identify the best item from a sequence. Finally, we introduce a generalized version of the secretary problem where an item can be rejected only if a subsequently observed item is strictly superior, and we solve this variant using our main theorem. This approach demonstrates that the optimal stopping rule involves skipping the first $k$ items, where $k$ corresponds to the item currently in the lead, and selecting the first item thereafter that exceeds all preceding ones. Consequently, the optimal strategy is not necessarily to pursue the absolute best item, but rather to target the second-best. As the number of items approaches infinity, the probability of winning approaches $1/e$, identical to the standard secretary problem, yet the probability of securing the second-best item converges to $1/(e^2/4) \approx 0.541$, which is more than twice as high.

This study introduces a transparent deep learning framework for low-dose CT denoising that combines a convolutional neural network (CNN) with a residual learning component. The CNN is trained to predict the difference between the original and noisy images, serving as the residual for a CNN-based image-to-image translator. This approach ensures data trustworthiness by leveraging the interpretability of CNNs and guarantees imaging quality through the superior performance of the main translator. Furthermore, the transparent model outperforms both the black-box CNN and end-to-end deep learning methods in terms of clinical features. The study concludes that this new framework offers a promising solution for low-dose CT denoising by effectively balancing clinical features and imaging quality.

This study introduces a straightforward yet effective approach to adapt state-of-the-art large-scale unsupervised contrastive learning models to settings with limited batch sizes. Our methodology involves two primary steps: (1) integrating an auxiliary memory bank into existing contrastive learning frameworks to enable the utilization of virtual samples even when batches are small, and (2) developing a novel parameter update strategy that leverages predictions from contrastive loss computed on these virtual samples. Extensive experiments conducted across various datasets and batch sizes show that our approach achieves performance comparable to methods trained with massive batches while requiring significantly fewer computational resources. Specifically, our model trained with a batch size of 256 matches the accuracy of a model trained with 65,536 samples while consuming approximately 25 times less computation. Furthermore, our model trained with a batch size of 2,048 outperforms the one trained with 65,536 samples. Additionally, we demonstrate that our update strategy effectively improves other popular self-supervised methods, such as SimCLR and MoCo, when trained with small batches. Our code is available at https://github.com/zhengyilong/SmallBatch-Pretraining.

**Summary:** This paper presents a simple yet effective method for adapting state-of-the-art, large-scale unsupervised contrastive learning models to limited batch sizes. By adding an auxiliary memory bank and employing a new parameter update strategy that uses virtual samples, our approach achieves comparable performance to models trained with vastly larger batches while consuming roughly 25 times less computation.

Introduction

This work examines the foundational connections between the diagonal lemma and the initial stages of Godel's incompleteness proof. Specifically, it explores how the diagonal lemma functions as a fixed point tool that generates both Godel's First Incompleteness Theorem and Tarski's Undefinability Theorem. Furthermore, we observe that the diagonal lemma itself is a direct consequence of the more fundamental First Fixed Point Theorem.

Godel's Incompleteness Theorems represent a landmark achievement in mathematical logic, demonstrating that any sufficiently powerful formal system cannot simultaneously be both complete and consistent. The original proofs, delivered by K. Godel in 1931, relied on arithmetization and the arithmetical representability of recursive functions. These methods enabled the construction of a self-referential statement asserting its own unprovability within the system.

Godel's original demonstration of the existence of this unprovable, self-unprovable statement constitutes the first application of the diagonal lemma. This specific instance is an example of the broader First Fixed Point Theorem, which asserts that for any decidable set of natural numbers, there exists a natural number that either does not belong to the set or is not the result of applying the diagonalization function to a number within the set.

The outer loop employs a random sampler to generate initial poses, while the inner loop refines these estimates using 2D-3D pose optimization. To ensure robustness, the technique incorporates a RANSAC algorithm to filter out incorrect initial pose estimates. To mitigate the impact of background noise and occlusions, the system relies on 3D bounding boxes derived from a pre-trained 3D object detector. Validation across two real-world assembly scenarios—mounting a battery and installing a bracket—demonstrates that the technique achieves high accuracy, with mean absolute errors of 0.65 cm and 0.42 cm, respectively. The complete implementation is available on GitHub. The core contributions of this work are: (1) a novel eye-in-hand camera calibration technique based on assembly tasks, (2) a robust 2D-3D pose optimization method designed to handle background clutter and occlusions, and (3) a dual-loop optimization strategy for enhancing pose estimation accuracy. The primary limitation of this technique is its dependence on 3D bounding box detection, which may yield inaccurate results for objects with complex geometries. Future enhancements could involve incorporating more features from 3D CAD models to improve detection performance. The primary audience for this research includes robotics engineers, computer vision specialists, and assembly system designers. Keywords: Eye-in-hand camera calibration, 2D-3D pose optimization, 3D bounding box, assembly.

Introduction

This paper provides an exhaustive analysis of invariant lines and planes within cubic polynomials. Our approach involves identifying the conditions under which these lower-dimensional invariants exist and determining their specific locations. While the case of invariant lines has been thoroughly addressed in prior research, our investigation of invariant planes reveals that, to the best of our knowledge, no complete characterization currently exists in the literature.

Cubic polynomials represent the simplest class of dynamical systems capable of exhibiting complex behavior, including the presence of a limit cycle. Consequently, they serve as a valuable model for exploring the onset of such complexity. Our primary objective is to examine invariant lines and planes in cubic polynomials, addressing a problem that remains unresolved in existing literature.

The concept of invariant manifolds is essential for comprehending the behavior of trajectories near hyperbolic fixed points. Specifically, the stable and unstable manifolds of a hyperbolic fixed point correspond to the invariant manifolds of the linearized system at that point.

While an atmosphere can be replenished via outgassing, a magnetic field is generated by a dynamo in a metallic core, which depends on the balance between heat loss from the core and the cooling rate of the mantle. This research underscores the necessity of considering both atmospheric and magnetic factors when assessing the habitability of exoplanets. ### 1 Introduction

Locating sound sources in the wild is a challenging task that has garnered significant attention in recent years. Existing methods typically depend on audio input from external sensors, such as microphones, to determine the position of visible sound sources. However, these approaches are often expensive and may fail in scenarios where audio data is unavailable. Consequently, there is a critical need for techniques that can infer sound locations using only visual input.

In this work, we introduce the first method capable of determining the position of visible sound sources using solely visual data. Our approach is grounded in the observation that an object emitting sound casts an occlusion shadow on surrounding items, as illustrated in Figure 1. Since the set of occluding objects varies depending on the sound source's position, the resulting pattern of shadows serves as a distinctive signature. Therefore, the position estimation problem can be framed as learning to recognize these specific occlusion signatures.

We validate our approach through qualitative experiments and demonstrate its utility in finding the location of a playing musical instrument. To achieve this, we employ a bottom-up saliency method to identify potential occlusion signatures and a classifier to differentiate genuine signatures from background noise. Our findings indicate that this method effectively identifies occlusion signatures and successfully locates the instrument.

The study of quantum gravity remains an active area of research, with significant efforts dedicated to understanding the theory's non-perturbative nature. A primary objective is to establish a UV-complete description of quantum gravity, potentially through a formulation like asymptotic safety. While this has been achieved for the Einstein-Hilbert action, extending it to include matter and additional gravitational interactions remains a challenge. To advance this goal, it is essential to perform higher-order calculations, such as the two-loop level. However, performing these computations using the traditional Feynman diagram method is currently infeasible. Therefore, employing the background field method to streamline these calculations is crucial. This paper introduces and demonstrates that approach using a simple example.

We demonstrate that the background field method, when combined with the use of master integrals, can substantially simplify computations in quantum field theory. This combination is particularly advantageous for the background field approach, as it allows for the selection of a gauge that minimizes the number of distinct integrands needed. This selection reduces the number of independent master integrals by a factor of three, making previously unfeasible calculations possible. As an illustration, we apply this technique to determine the one-loop self-energy of the graviton. This result matches the expected outcome derived from traditional Feynman diagrams. This methodology is directly applicable to other quantum field theories, including the Standard Model and the Higgs Effective Field Theory. The corresponding code is available on GitHub.

This work demonstrates that a specific set of thermodynamic operations involving negative temperature enables the complete conversion of heat into mechanical work across any positive efficiency. These findings highlight the exceptional capabilities of negative temperature states in thermodynamic cycles, such as the Carnot engine, and provide a fresh perspective on the equivalence between heat and work. Recent advancements in nonequilibrium statistical mechanics have enabled the experimental realization of negative absolute temperature, a state once deemed physically impossible. This report presents a straightforward framework for analyzing such states, focusing on closed quantum systems with bounded energy spectra interacting with an environment at positive temperature. Within this model, we demonstrate the direct conversion of heat into work and provide a fresh perspective on the equivalence of these two forms of energy. These findings offer a clear understanding of the thermodynamic behavior of negative temperature states, particularly regarding the application of chemical pressure.

We examine the thermodynamic properties of a charged, rotating, asymptotically anti-de Sitter black hole in four dimensions when its matter fields are in negative temperature. By employing the standard canonical ensemble, we derive key characteristics such as heat capacity, specific volume, and compressibility. Our analysis reveals the existence of first-order phase transitions and critical points, alongside regions of negative specific heat, volume, and compressibility. Notably, we find that both positive and negative temperatures can coexist at identical temperatures and pressures, and that negative temperature states can achieve any positive efficiency. These results indicate that negative absolute temperature is not merely a theoretical curiosity but a physically attainable state with significant implications for black hole thermodynamics.

Initially, we transform the problem into an equivalent formulation featuring a specific time-decaying harmonic series of Dirichlet data on the obstacle's boundary. Subsequently, we apply an accelerated collocation method to resolve this transformed equation, yielding a solution to the original problem. Finally, we demonstrate how to incorporate time-domain source terms into the method, allowing for simulations of wave propagation and scattering driven by localized sources. This represents the first instance of simulating electromagnetic wave scattering off an irregular obstacle in three dimensions with both high fidelity and memory efficiency. The K-2 OIB exhibits a distinct geochemical signature, characterized by high incompatible element concentrations and a lack of subducted sediment components. Our analyses of glass samples from the Kerguelen Plateau indicate that the K-2 source contains approximately 10 parts per million (ppm) of water, which is roughly 20% of the water content found in wet eclogite. Additionally, the K-2 isotopic composition is notably depleted in deuterium, with a $\delta D$ value of -150 per mil (‰), which is 100‰ lower than that of ocean water. These findings suggest that the K-2 source is a mixture of depleted mantle and a wet component derived from ocean water. We propose that this wet component was introduced into the depleted mantle during the early stages of Earth's history, likely through the subduction of oceanic crust and/or the direct injection of rainwater into the ocean basins. The K-2 OIB represents the first documented case of an ocean island basalt originating from a mantle source with such low water content and highly depleted hydrogen isotopic signature. This discovery challenges the conventional view that all subducted sediments and/or rainwater are required to explain the geochemical heterogeneity of the Earth's mantle. Furthermore, the presence of this distinct mantle component supports the existence of a long-lived, isolated reservoir within the Earth's interior. Finally, the mixing of this component with the depleted mantle offers a potential explanation for the origin of the HIMU (high $^{206}$Pb/$^{204}$Pb) mantle component.

Although the integration of audio into translation processes has significantly enhanced source language text-to-text translation quality, it has also yielded improvements in speech translation. Nevertheless, these systems often depend on extensive, perfectly aligned, parallel training data comprising utterances in all target languages. Despite the clear advantages of ST, gathering such fully aligned, parallel datasets across multiple target languages remains a significant challenge. This paper introduces a novel approach to cross-lingual speech translation that leverages monolingual audio data for each target language instead of requiring parallel corpora. By employing an attention-based mechanism, our method effectively incorporates monolingual audio data, automatically aligning and integrating it with text-to-text translation models. Experimental results demonstrate that our proposed approach achieves performance comparable to systems trained on parallel data while offering greater cost-effectiveness and efficiency. Additionally, the system shows superior results in scenarios where only a limited amount of parallel data is available. By utilizing a two-orbital model where spins on A and B sublattices are decoupled, we examine how SOC influences low-lying excitations near the charge neutrality point. Our analysis of both spin-resolved and spin-degenerated systems reveals that SOC induces level crossings between excitations from different many-body configurations, thereby generating an effective exchange interaction. Specifically, in the half-filled case, this interaction is antiferromagnetic and scales with the square of the SOC strength. Furthermore, we observe that the nature of the excitation spectrum at the edges of the many-body energy bands is highly sensitive to SOC. In degenerate spin systems, SOC drives a transition from a quadratic to a linear dependence of excitation energy on momentum. Conversely, in systems with degenerate total spin, the initially linear dependence persists. We also determine the precise dependence of the slope of this linear dispersion on the strength of the SOC. These findings offer valuable insights into the excitation dynamics of charge-neutral graphene under strong magnetic fields and SOC, which are crucial for the design of spin-orbit quantum Hall devices. Additionally, our results on the momentum dependence of excitations in neutral graphene support the interpretation of recent experimental data regarding the effective mass of charge carriers in graphene under SOC. Finally, our study of the exchange interaction in half-filled graphene provides a quantitative basis for the effective mass of charge carriers in the quantum Hall effect of graphene with SOC, as reported in recent experiments.

In this work, we develop a two-orbital model to investigate the impact of spin-orbit coupling (SOC) on the quantum Hall effect in graphene. We derive an effective exchange interaction arising from SOC and apply it to analyze the excitation spectrum of a half-filled graphene system. Our results indicate that in the long-wavelength limit, the excitation energy exhibits linear dispersion, implying that the effective mass of charge carriers in a half-filled graphene system with SOC is zero. This contrasts with the zero-SOC scenario, where the effective mass is twice that of free electrons. These conclusions are consistent with recent experimental findings.

We establish that for smooth projective varieties sharing the same dimension, the relative quantum cohomology of the quotient map from $X$ to the generic fiber of a morphism $f: X \to S$ is isomorphic to that of $X$ itself, provided the generic fiber of $f$ is irreducible. Additionally, we demonstrate that relative quantum $K$-theory remains invariant under birational transformations. These findings yield new proofs of the equivalence between relative quantum cohomology and quantum $K$-theory, as well as their invariance under proper torus-equivariant deformations. The analysis relies on the theory of categorical $J$-functions and the categorical $I$-function. As a byproduct, we provide a combinatorial interpretation for relative quantum $K$-theory using stable $K$-theory sheaves. This combinatorial perspective enables us to establish the invariance of relative quantum $K$-theory under proper torus-equivariant deformations. Finally, we explore the relationship between relative quantum $K$-theory and $K$-theory of the total space of a deformation. The combinatorial approach presented here is expected to facilitate the study of $K$-theoretic invariants under more general birational transformations. Most existing approaches achieve this by training a disentanglement network on an unstructured dataset of individual images. In contrast, we examine the potential of leveraging structured photo collections, such as those found in online photo albums, to enhance GAN-based image style transfer and editing. By incorporating photo albums, our approach offers two key advantages: (1) it provides contextually relevant examples for modifying an image's style, and (2) it enables the creation of image pairs with consistent content within the latent space. Consequently, our method facilitates more effective and targeted image editing. We introduce a novel framework called AlbumGAN, which performs content-based image translation by predicting the latent code for the target style. We assess our method against various baseline techniques across multiple datasets and demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms current state-of-the-art methods in both qualitative and quantitative evaluations. Furthermore, we provide a web-based demo at http://demo.sungyupark.com/albumgan/ to allow users to interact with our algorithm. Our source code is available at https://github.com/sungyupark/AlbumGAN. In conclusion, photo albums serve as an accessible and practical resource for improving generative image editing. Our algorithm achieves superior results in closed-loop translation and proves highly effective for within-class translation. The web demo allows for easy comparison with baseline methods. Additionally, we show that latent codes can be predicted with high accuracy, enabling precise and targeted image editing. Finally, we confirm that album-based training is a practical and efficient strategy for enhancing image translation and editing tasks.

While numerous tools exist for analyzing and visualizing video, and some support object tracking and ReID, there remains a lack of solutions designed for voluminous life-long video data. ViDaExpert fills this gap by offering features for visualizing and analyzing life-long trajectories of object instances. These capabilities include filtering and visualizing trajectories by location, time, and class, as well as displaying instance-wise ReID results to identify the same objects across different contexts. A demo system is available at https://alexander-krueger.github.io/VidaExpert/.

Life-long video data encompasses extensive collections of recordings from the same environment, captured over extended periods using one or more cameras. This type of data is frequently employed to train and evaluate algorithms for visual recognition and tracking. Although various tools are present for visualizing and analyzing such datasets, they often require specialized knowledge to utilize effectively. Furthermore, existing solutions typically lack integrated support for visualizing object tracking and ReID data. ViDaExpert addresses these limitations by providing a user-friendly interface for visualizing and analyzing life-long video data with respect to tracked object instances. It enables the visualization and analysis of life-long trajectories, supports filtering and visualizing them by time and location, and allows for the examination of instance-wise ReID results to identify the same objects across different times and places. The demo system can be found at https://alexander-krueger.github.io/VidaExpert/.

large-scale structures is a fundamental yet difficult task in cosmological simulations. While the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) offers a general solution for solving Poisson's equation, its application to Newtonian potentials in this context remains limited. This study introduces a hierarchical particle-mesh FMM algorithm designed to calculate Newtonian potentials for all particles in an N-body system. The algorithm incorporates both periodic and non-periodic boundary conditions to accommodate various simulation environments. Additionally, it features a novel non-periodic solver for the multipole expansion potential that utilizes the Euler-Titchmarsh formula for potential accuracy. Benchmark tests were conducted on a high-performance computing cluster using datasets ranging from $10^6$ to $10^8$ particles. The results indicate that the proposed algorithm is highly efficient, achieving a speedup of approximately 100 times compared to the conventional particle-mesh FMM when applied to $10^8$ particles. Furthermore, the algorithm demonstrates superior performance in scenarios involving large voids or void-like regions. These findings suggest that the proposed method is both highly efficient and broadly applicable for computing Newtonian potentials in N-body simulations. The algorithm's source code is publicly accessible at https://github.com/ChenWen1998/Particle-mesh_FMM.

The calculation of Newtonian potentials is essential for simulating gravitational interactions among particles. In N-body simulations, the standard approach involves directly solving Newton's equations of motion, which requires computing the gravitational force generated by every other particle for each individual particle. This direct method becomes computationally prohibitive as the number of particles increases. To address this, alternative techniques such as the particle-mesh method and the Fast Multipole Method (FMM) have been developed. This study examines these methods and presents a hierarchical particle-mesh FMM algorithm for determining Newtonian potentials.

The paper is organized as follows: Section \ref{sec:NM} reviews the direct method for calculating Newtonian potentials. Section \ref{sec:PM} details the particle-mesh method, covering mesh generation, potential calculation, and force derivation. Section \ref{sec:FMM} explains the FMM, including its core operations, periodic and non-periodic boundary condition solvers, and the computation of Newtonian potentials. Section \ref{sec:PMFMM} describes the proposed particle-mesh FMM algorithm. Section \ref{sec:exp} presents the experimental setup, and Section \ref{sec:con} provides the conclusions.
